# 6.8 Uncertainty, Significant Figures and Dimensional Analysis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two laboratory skills sit alongside the theory of this chapter: knowing how far to trust a measurement, and knowing how to check that an equation makes sense at all.

## Uncertainty

Measurements in chemistry might be inaccurate by eye. This creates **uncertainty** — being unsure of the exact value of something.

The uncertainty is calculated as **half of the scale graduations**. A burette marked every $0.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ therefore carries an uncertainty of $0.05\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, because that is the finest distinction the scale allows you to make by eye.

## Error

To evaluate the accuracy of experimental data, calculate the difference between the experimental value and the accepted value:

$$\text{Error} = \text{experimental value} - \text{accepted value}$$

Error can be negative. The sign is information — it tells you which side of the accepted value you fell on — so do not discard it.

## Systematic and random error

**Systematic error** comes from procedures, methods or theories. Its sources include:

- an incorrectly zeroed balance
- poorly calibrated or badly made instruments
- instrument parallax error — reading a scale from a position that is not directly in front of the scale
- improper conditions

**Systematic errors cannot be reduced by repetition.** If the balance reads high every time, averaging a hundred readings only gives you a very precise wrong answer.

The error associated with estimating the last digit of a reading is called **random uncertainty**. Random uncertainties arise mostly from limitations in the instrument.

## Percentage uncertainty

The **percentage uncertainty** changes with the amount of material that you are measuring. The absolute uncertainty of a piece of apparatus is fixed by its scale, so measuring a larger quantity with the same apparatus makes that fixed uncertainty a smaller fraction of the result.

Percentage uncertainty is also a guiding factor in choosing equipment for an experiment — it is the quantity you compare when deciding which instrument is good enough for the measurement you need.

## Dimensional analysis

**Dimensions** are the fundamental types of physical quantities.

The main idea of **dimensional analysis** is to check the consistency of equations and to help in deriving relationships between physical quantities. It is like a grammar check for the language of physics and engineering equations: an equation whose two sides do not carry the same dimensions cannot be right, whatever the numbers say.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uncertainty** | Being unsure of the exact value of something; calculated as half of the scale graduations |
| **Error** | The experimental value minus the accepted value; can be negative |
| **Systematic error** | Error coming from procedures, methods or theories; it cannot be reduced by repetition |
| **Parallax error** | Reading a scale from a position that is not directly in front of the scale |
| **Random uncertainty** | The error associated with estimating the last digit of a reading; arises mostly from limitations in the instrument |
| **Percentage uncertainty** | An uncertainty expressed as a percentage; it changes with the amount of material being measured and guides the choice of equipment |
| **Dimensions** | The fundamental types of physical quantities |
| **Dimensional analysis** | Checking the consistency of equations and deriving relationships between physical quantities |

# 7.1 Development of the Periodic Table

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The periodic table was not designed; it was noticed. The story below is a sequence in which each step supplies something the previous step was missing.

## The elements are counted

In the **1790s**, Antoine Lavoisier compiled a list of 23 elements known at the time. By **1870** there were approximately 70 known elements.

That growth is what made organisation urgent. Twenty-three substances can simply be listed; seventy cannot be held in the head without some structure.

## Atomic mass becomes measurable

In the **1860s**, chemists developed and agreed upon a method of determining the atomic mass of elements.

This is the enabling step for everything that follows. Without an agreed method there is no shared quantity to order the elements by, and so no way to see a pattern.

## Newlands sees a repetition

In **1864**, John Newlands observed the repetition of properties in every eight elements. This demonstrates a **periodic** change, because it repeats in a specific manner.

## Mendeleev and Meyer

In **1869**, Dmitri Mendeleev and Lothar Meyer both demonstrated a connection between atomic mass and elemental properties.

Mendeleev was given more credit because he was the earliest to publish his organisation plan and demonstrated how it was useful. Priority of publication and demonstrated usefulness, rather than the discovery itself, are what separate the two names.

Mendeleev noticed that **when the elements were ordered by increasing atomic mass, there was a repetition, or periodic pattern, in their chemical and physical properties.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Periodic change** | A change that repeats in a specific manner, as with the repetition of properties Newlands observed in every eight elements |

title: Effective Nuclear Charge and the Sizes of Atoms and Ions
summary: One quantity drives the periodic trends in this chapter. Establish it first and the size trends fall out of it. Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge experienced by the valence electrons
markdown:
# 7.2 Effective Nuclear Charge and the Sizes of Atoms and Ions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

One quantity drives the periodic trends in this chapter. Establish it first and the size trends fall out of it.

## Effective nuclear charge

**Effective nuclear charge** is the net positive charge experienced by the valence electrons, accounting for the nuclear charge and the shielding by inner electrons.

Its trends:

| Direction | Effective nuclear charge |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Increases |
| Down a group | Increases slightly |

The contrast between "increases" and "increases slightly" is the important part. Across a period the nucleus gains protons while the shielding inner shell stays the same, so the valence electrons feel much more pull. Down a group protons are added too, but so is a whole new shielding layer, so the net gain is small.

## Atomic radius

| Direction | Atomic radius |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Decreases |
| Down a group | Increases |

The across-a-period result is the counterintuitive one, and it is exactly what the effective nuclear charge predicts: adding electrons to the same shell while the effective nuclear charge rises pulls that shell in tighter, so the atom gets smaller.

## Ionic radius

**Cations are smaller than their parent atoms**, because the loss of electrons reduces repulsion. Fewer electrons in the cloud means less pushing apart, and the remainder are drawn in closer.

## Isoelectronic series

In an **isoelectronic series** — species with the same number of electrons — size decreases with increasing nuclear charge. With the electron count held fixed, the only variable left is how hard the nucleus pulls, so the species with the most protons is the smallest.

## Worked example

Which is the largest atom among $\mathrm{Na}$, $\mathrm{Be}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}$?

$\mathrm{Na}$ — it is in Group 1 and Period 3. It sits furthest down and furthest left of the three, which is the corner in which both trends point towards the largest radius.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Effective nuclear charge** | The net positive charge experienced by valence electrons, accounting for nuclear charge and shielding by inner electrons |
| **Atomic radius** | The size of an atom; decreases across a period and increases down a group |
| **Ionic radius** | The size of an ion; cations are smaller than their parent atoms because losing electrons reduces repulsion |
| **Isoelectronic series** | A set of species in which size decreases with increasing nuclear charge |

# 7.4 Ionisation Energy, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Three quantities describe how an atom handles electrons: what it costs to take one away, what happens when one is added, and how hard it pulls on the electrons in a bond it has already formed.

## Ionisation energy

**Ionisation energy** is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. The "gaseous" condition matters — it fixes the atom as isolated, so the value measures the atom itself and not its neighbours.

| Direction | Ionisation energy |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Increases |
| Down a group | Decreases |

Both follow the effective nuclear charge: a more strongly held electron is a more expensive electron to remove.

### The exception

There is a break in the across-a-period increase **between Groups IIA and IIIA** — for example $\mathrm{Be} > \mathrm{B}$, where the later element has the *lower* ionisation energy.

The reason is which electron is being removed. In Group IIIA the electron taken out is a p electron, which sits at higher energy, whereas in Group IIA it is an s electron. A higher-energy electron is less tightly bound, so removing it costs less even though the nuclear charge has gone up.

## Electron affinity

**Electron affinity** is the energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom. It is the mirror image of ionisation energy: one measures adding an electron to an isolated atom, the other removing one.

## Electronegativity

**Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to attract electrons in a bond.

| Direction | Electronegativity |
|---|---|
| Across a period | Increases |
| Down a group | Decreases |

The across-a-period increase is again the effective nuclear charge at work — a higher effective nuclear charge means a stronger pull on any electron nearby, including one being shared in a bond.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ionisation energy** | The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom |
| **Electron affinity** | The energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom |
| **Electronegativity** | The ability of an atom to attract electrons in a bond |

# 8.1 Lewis Symbols and the Octet Rule

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a chemical bond is

A **chemical bond** is the electrostatic attraction force that holds two atoms together. All three bond types below are versions of that one idea; they differ only in which charged things are being attracted to which.

| Bond type | Attraction between |
|---|---|
| **Ionic bond** | Cations and anions |
| **Covalent bond** | The nucleus and shared electrons |
| **Metallic bond** | Metal cations and delocalised electrons |

## The octet rule

The **octet rule** is the tendency for electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration — "octet" refers to 8 valence electrons.

This is the rule that predicts what an atom will do in a bond: whether it gives electrons away, takes them, or shares them depends on which route gets it to a noble gas configuration fastest.

## Lewis symbols

**Lewis symbols** are a drawing method that serves as an alternative to electron configuration. They are used to express chemical bonding and molecular geometry and to demonstrate valence.

To draw one:

1. Write the element — for example $\mathrm{H}$.
2. Determine the number of valence electrons — $\mathrm{H}$ has 1.
3. Draw one dot for each valence electron. For $\mathrm{H}$, with only one valence electron, only one dot is needed.
4. For most cases, the valence electrons should be as spread out on the four sides of the letter as possible. This is Hund's rule applied to the drawing: electrons occupy separate positions before they pair up.

Exceptions to the spreading rule are not considered in the test.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Chemical bond** | The electrostatic attraction force that holds two atoms together |
| **Ionic bond** | Attraction between cations and anions |
| **Covalent bond** | Attraction between the nucleus and shared electrons |
| **Metallic bond** | Attraction between metal cations and delocalised electrons |
| **Octet rule** | The tendency for electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration, "octet" referring to 8 valence electrons |
| **Lewis symbols** | A drawing method alternative to electron configuration, used to express chemical bonding and molecular geometry and to demonstrate valence |

markdown:
# 8.2 Ionic Bonding

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why ions form

Because of the octet rule, atoms want to gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas configuration.

| Action | Result | Charge |
|---|---|---|
| Losing electrons | Cation | Positive |
| Gaining electrons | Anion | Negative |

Which way an atom goes is decided by whichever is the shorter route. Halogens (Group 17) have 7 valence electrons and need only 1 more to complete the octet, so they most often appear as anions with a $1-$ charge.

> **Tip for the test:** check the periodic table before you do bonding questions. The group number tells you the valence count, and the valence count tells you the charge.

## The pseudo-noble gas exception

For elements from Group 1B through 4A in Periods 4 to 6, the ions form by adopting a **pseudo-noble gas notation**, which is relatively stable as well. Examples include $\mathrm{Zn}$, $\mathrm{Pb}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$.

These elements do not reach a true noble gas configuration, but the arrangement they do reach is stable enough to be the one that forms.

## Ionic compounds

An **ionic compound** can be described simply as the bond between cations and anions. The cations give electrons to the anions, creating an electrostatic force that bonds the two together.

Ionic compounds **must be neutral** — the charges of the cations and anions must balance. This is the constraint that fixes the formula: it is why the compound of a $2+$ cation and a $1-$ anion has two anions per cation and not one.

> **Tip for the test:** when asked to explain trends of ionic bonds, refer to Coulomb's Law.

## Lattice structures

Ionic compounds exist in groups. When they are grouped together the pattern is always $+-+-+-\ldots$, which makes it look like a lattice — a **lattice structure**.

## Properties

- Ionic compounds have a **high melting point** and **hardness**.
- Ionic compounds are **brittle**.

Both properties trace back to the same alternating lattice. The regular $+-+-$ arrangement means every ion is surrounded by oppositely charged neighbours, which is a great deal of electrostatic attraction to overcome — hence the high melting point and hardness. But the arrangement is also rigid, which is why a force that disturbs it shatters the solid rather than bending it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cation** | An ion formed by losing electrons, carrying a positive charge |
| **Anion** | An ion formed by gaining electrons, carrying a negative charge |
| **Pseudo-noble gas notation** | The relatively stable configuration adopted by ions of elements from Group 1B through 4A in Periods 4 to 6, such as $\mathrm{Zn}$, $\mathrm{Pb}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$ |
| **Ionic compound** | The bond between cations and anions, in which cations give electrons to anions and an electrostatic force bonds the two together |
| **Lattice structure** | The $+-+-+-$ pattern formed when ionic compounds are grouped together |

# 8.3 Covalent Bonds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Before starting, review the definition of valence electrons — the whole of covalent bonding is an account of what those electrons do when neither atom is willing to hand them over.

## When covalent bonding happens

Covalent bonding occurs when atoms have quite high electronegativities. Neither atom will surrender an electron outright, so the electrons are shared instead.

> **Critical thinking:** given that, what properties do the elements involved in covalent bonds have?

The guide also sets out the general trend in how many covalent bonds different elements form, and asks: what conclusion can you draw from that trend?

## Sigma and pi bonds

Covalent bonds are classified by shape into **sigma ($\sigma$)** and **pi ($\pi$)** bonds.

**Sigma bonds** have the overlap of electrons focused on the intermolecular axis. The electron density is concentrated in the middle, directly between the two nuclei.

**Pi bonds** only occur in p orbitals. The p shells overlap vertically, forming two sausage-shaped clouds of electrons parallel to the intermolecular axis.

**Pi bonds have less energy because they have more repulsion.** The electron density in a $\pi$ bond sits off to the sides rather than between the nuclei, so the arrangement is less favourable than the head-on overlap of a $\sigma$ bond.

## Multiple bonds

Covalent bonds can exist as double or triple bonds. Every bond between two atoms contains exactly one $\sigma$ bond; the extra bonds of a multiple bond are all $\pi$.

| Bond | Composition |
|---|---|
| Single | 1 $\sigma$ |
| Double | 1 $\sigma$ + 1 $\pi$ |
| Triple | 1 $\sigma$ + 2 $\pi$ |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sigma ($\sigma$) bond** | A bond whose electron overlap is focused on the intermolecular axis, with the electron density in the middle |
| **Pi ($\pi$) bond** | A bond occurring only in p orbitals, where the p shells overlap vertically to form two sausage-shaped clouds of electrons parallel to the intermolecular axis; it has less energy than a sigma bond because it has more repulsion |

# 8.4 Bond Polarity and Electronegativity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Bond polarity

**Bond polarity** is a measure of how equally or unequally the electrons in any covalent bond are shared. In a **polar covalent bond**, one of the atoms exerts a greater attraction for the bonding electrons than the other.

**Polarity** refers to a separation of positive and negative charge.

- In a **nonpolar bond**, the bonding electrons are shared equally — diatomic molecules are the clearest case, since the two atoms are identical and neither can out-pull the other.
- In a **polar bond**, electrons are shared unequally.

## Electronegativity

In general, electronegativity values **decrease from top to bottom** and **increase from left to right**.

> **Test tip:** do not explain questions through direct trends. Focus instead on the reasons behind the trends — that requires critical thinking, and it is what the question is actually testing.

## Using the electronegativity difference

The electronegativity difference on the Pauling scale determines the type of bond:

| $\Delta EN$ | Bond type |
|---|---|
| $> 2.0$ | Ionic |
| $0.4 - 2.0$ | Polar covalent |
| $< 0.4$ | Nonpolar covalent |

The boundaries make sense as a continuum rather than three separate phenomena: a large enough difference in pulling power means one atom has effectively taken the electrons rather than shared them, which is an ionic bond.

## Dipole moments

A positive-to-negative partial charge in an atom is measured as its **dipole moment**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Bond polarity** | A measure of how equally or unequally the electrons in any covalent bond are shared |
| **Polar covalent bond** | A bond in which one of the atoms exerts a greater attraction for the bonding electrons than the other |
| **Polarity** | A separation of positive and negative charge |
| **Nonpolar bond** | A bond in which the bonding electrons are shared equally |
| **Dipole moment** | The measure of a positive-to-negative partial charge in an atom |

# 8.5 Drawing Lewis Structures

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Starting the structure

**Step 1: calculate the total valence electrons.** Everything that follows is an exercise in distributing that fixed total, so getting the count wrong at the start makes the rest of the work worthless no matter how careful it is.

## Formal charge

Once a structure is drawn, **formal charge** tells you whether it is a good one:

$$\text{Formal charge} = \text{valence } e^- - \left( \frac{\text{bonding } e^-}{2} + \text{nonbonding } e^- \right)$$

Bonding electrons are halved because they are shared between two atoms; nonbonding electrons belong entirely to the atom that carries them, so they count in full.

### Choosing the best structure

Two rules select between competing structures:

- **Minimise the charges.**
- **Place negative charges on the electronegative atoms.**

The second follows from what electronegativity means: an electronegative atom is the one that attracts electrons, so it is the one that can carry extra negative charge most comfortably.

## Examples

**$\mathrm{CO_2}$** is drawn as $\mathrm{O=C=O}$. The formal charges are $\mathrm{C} = 0$ and $\mathrm{O} = 0$ throughout — every atom carries zero, which is as close to the "minimise the charges" ideal as a structure can get.

**$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$** is drawn as $\mathrm{O=N-O^-}$, and it has a resonance structure with the double bond shifting position. That behaviour is the subject of the next section.

## Practice

Draw Lewis structures for:

- $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$
- $\mathrm{HCN}$
- $\mathrm{ClO_2^-}$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Formal charge** | Valence electrons minus the sum of half the bonding electrons and all the nonbonding electrons |

summary: Two sections here, and both are about the same admission: a single Lewis structure obeying the octet rule does not always describe a real molecule. Resonance structures are multiple valid Lewis struct
markdown:
# 8.6 Resonance Structures and Exceptions to the Octet Rule

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Two sections here, and both are about the same admission: a single Lewis structure obeying the octet rule does not always describe a real molecule.

## Resonance structures

**Resonance structures** are multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule or ion, arising from delocalised electrons.

### Ozone, $\mathrm{O_3}$

$$\mathrm{O=O-O} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{O-O=O}$$

The measurement that settles the matter: **both $\mathrm{O-O}$ bonds are $1.28\ \text{Å}$** — shorter than a single bond but longer than a double bond. Neither drawn structure is what the molecule actually is. The real molecule is a single thing in which the electrons are spread over both bonds, so both bonds come out intermediate in length.

### Carbonate, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$

The carbonate ion is drawn with one double bond and two single $\mathrm{O^-}$ bonds, and there are two other resonance forms in which the double bond shifts to a different oxygen.

### Practice

Identify resonance structures for $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$.

## Exceptions to the octet rule

There are three kinds.

### 1. Odd number of electrons

Molecules with unpaired electrons cannot have every atom at eight, because eight is even and the total available is not.

Examples: $\mathrm{NO}$, $\mathrm{ClO_2}$.

For $\mathrm{NO}$: $\mathrm{N}$ has 5 valence electrons and $\mathrm{O}$ has 6, giving a total of 11 — an odd number, so at least one electron must be left unpaired.

### 2. Fewer than 8 electrons (incomplete octet)

Elements like $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{Be}$ may form compounds with fewer than 8 electrons.

Example: in $\mathrm{BF_3}$, boron has 6 electrons from its three single bonds to fluorine.

### 3. Expanded octet

Elements in Period 3 and beyond — such as $\mathrm{P}$, $\mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}$ — can use d orbitals to hold more than 8 electrons. The period restriction is the key: Period 2 elements have no d orbitals available, which is why this exception never applies to them.

Example: in $\mathrm{PCl_5}$, phosphorus has 10 electrons from its five single bonds to chlorine.

### Practice

Classify the exceptions to the octet rule in $\mathrm{XeF_4}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ and $\mathrm{NO}$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Resonance structures** | Multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule or ion, due to delocalised electrons |
| **Incomplete octet** | An exception in which elements such as $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{Be}$ form compounds with fewer than 8 electrons |
| **Expanded octet** | An exception in which elements in Period 3 and beyond use d orbitals to hold more than 8 electrons |

title: Naming Binary Molecular Compounds
summary: Binary molecular compounds are formed by nonmetal + nonmetal combinations — \mathrm{CO_2}, \mathrm{H_2O}, \mathrm{NH_3}. Unlike ionic compounds, they consist of discrete molecules, not formula units.
markdown:
# 9.1 Naming Binary Molecular Compounds

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What they are

**Binary molecular compounds** are formed by nonmetal + nonmetal combinations — $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$.

Unlike ionic compounds, they consist of **discrete molecules**, not formula units. That difference is what makes the naming system different: an ionic formula only states a ratio, so it needs no count, whereas a molecular formula states how many atoms are actually in the molecule, and the name has to say so.

## Naming rules

### Order of elements

1. Name the first element in the formula as the element name.
2. Name the second element using the root of the element name plus the suffix **-ide**, as with the anions of ionic compounds.

### Prefixes for atom count

Use prefixes to indicate the number of atoms of each element.

**Omit the prefix "mono-" for the first element if only one atom is present.** So $\mathrm{CO}$ is carbon monoxide, not "monocarbon monoxide".

The guide gives a table of prefixes to memorise, with the tip: **only memorise the table one day before the test.**

## From formula to name

1. Identify the elements in the formula. For $\mathrm{NF_3}$, these are nitrogen and fluorine.
2. Assign prefixes based on the number of atoms. Here $\mathrm{N} = 1$, so no prefix is used, since it is the first element.

## Common mistakes to avoid

**Confusing molecular with ionic compounds.** Molecular compounds never contain metal ions. $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ is ionic, not molecular; $\mathrm{PCl_3}$ is molecular. Checking whether a metal is present is the first thing to do, because it decides which naming system applies at all — and prefixes belong only to the molecular one.

**Incorrect prefix placement.** Always apply prefixes to both elements, except for "mono-" on the first element. So $\mathrm{N_2O}$ is dinitrogen monoxide, not "nitrogen monoxide".

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Binary molecular compound** | A compound formed by nonmetal + nonmetal combinations, consisting of discrete molecules rather than formula units |

title: Metallic Bonding and the Properties of Metals
summary: A metal has two key components: - Cations — positively charged metal ions formed by losing valence electrons, such as \mathrm{Na^+} and \mathrm{Mg^{2+}}. - The electron sea — delocalised valence elect
markdown:
# 9.2 Metallic Bonding and the Properties of Metals

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The atomic structure of metals

A metal has two key components:

- **Cations** — positively charged metal ions formed by losing valence electrons, such as $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$.
- The **electron sea** — delocalised valence electrons freely moving throughout the metal lattice.

The model analogy: think of the metal cations as islands submerged in a sea of electrons that hold them together.

## Physical properties explained by metallic bonding

Every property in the table is the electron sea doing something. Learn the explanations rather than the list — the questions ask why.

| Property | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Metallic lustre** | Free electrons absorb and re-emit light across the visible spectrum |
| **Conductivity** | Mobile electrons carry electric current (charge) and thermal energy (vibrations) |
| **Malleability** | Applying force causes cations to slide, but the electron sea prevents repulsion and breaking |
| **Ductility** | Cations can be drawn into wires without breaking bonds, supported by the electron sea |
| **High density** | Close-packed crystal structures, such as face-centred cubic, in most metals |

Malleability and ductility are the same mechanism seen twice: because the electrons are not tied to particular cations, moving the cations past each other never brings like charges face to face, so the metal deforms instead of shattering.

## The strength of metallic bonding

Two factors control it.

**1. Ionic radius.** A smaller radius means a stronger attraction to the electron sea. The radii increase in the order $\mathrm{Li^+} < \mathrm{Na^+} < \mathrm{K^+}$, so lithium's bonding is the strongest of the three.

**2. Number of valence electrons.** More electrons means stronger bonding: $\mathrm{Na}$ (1 e⁻) $<$ $\mathrm{Mg}$ (2 e⁻) $<$ $\mathrm{Al}$ (3 e⁻). More valence electrons donated means a denser electron sea holding the cations together.

### Worked question

**Why is magnesium's melting point ($650\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) higher than sodium's ($98\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$)?**

$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ has a smaller radius and more valence electrons (2 e⁻ against sodium's 1 e⁻), leading to stronger metallic bonding. Both factors point the same way, which is why the difference in melting point is so large.

## Metallic against ionic bonds

| Feature | Metallic bond | Ionic bond |
|---|---|---|
| Bonding particles | Cations + electron sea | Cations + anions (electrostatic attraction) |
| Electron movement | Delocalised (free to move) | Localised (fixed in lattice) |
| Conductivity (solid) | High (electrons mobile) | Low (ions fixed in place) |
| Mechanical behaviour | Malleable/ductile (flexible) | Brittle (shatters under force) |
| Examples | $\mathrm{Fe}$, $\mathrm{Cu}$, $\mathrm{Al}$ | $\mathrm{NaCl}$, $\mathrm{MgO}$ |

The last three rows all descend from the first. Whether the electrons can move decides whether the solid conducts, and whether the charged particles can slide past each other decides whether it bends or shatters.

## Alloys

**Alloys** are mixtures of metals — steel is $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{C}$. They enhance strength by disrupting the packing of the cations.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electron sea** | Delocalised valence electrons freely moving throughout the metal lattice |
| **Metallic lustre** | The shine of a metal, caused by free electrons absorbing and re-emitting light across the visible spectrum |
| **Malleability** | The ability to deform under force as cations slide, with the electron sea preventing repulsion and breaking |
| **Ductility** | The ability to be drawn into wires without breaking bonds, supported by the electron sea |
| **Alloy** | A mixture of metals, such as steel ($\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{C}$), which enhances strength by disrupting cation packing |

# 9.3 Molecular Geometry: VSEPR Theory and Applications

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The core principle

The aim of **VSEPR theory** is to predict three-dimensional molecular shapes by minimising repulsion between **electron domains**, both bonding and nonbonding.

Three rules govern it:

1. **Lone pair repulsion.** Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. Water's bent shape is the result of its 2 lone pairs.
2. **Double and triple bonds count as 1 electron domain.** $\mathrm{CO_2}$ has two double bonds, which is 2 domains, so the molecule is linear.
3. **Bond angle trends.** Lone pairs compress bond angles. Compare $\mathrm{NH_3}$ at $107°$ with $\mathrm{CH_4}$ at $109.5°$: both have four domains, but the lone pair in ammonia pushes the bonding pairs closer together.

Rule 2 is the one most often forgotten. A domain is a region of electron density, not a count of bonds, so a double bond occupies one region just as a single bond does.

## Step-by-step shape prediction

1. **Draw the Lewis structure.** Identify the central atom and count the valence electrons.
2. **Count electron domains.** Bonding domains equal the number of bonds, with single, double and triple bonds each counting as 1 domain. Add the lone pairs.
3. **Determine the electron domain geometry.** 2 domains give linear, 3 give trigonal planar, 4 give tetrahedral, and so on.
4. **Predict the molecular shape.** Ignore the lone pairs for the final shape — for example, 4 domains with 1 lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal.

Step 4 is where the two geometries part company. The lone pairs are still there and still repelling, which is why they set the domain geometry and squeeze the angles, but they are invisible when you name the shape because a shape is described by where the atoms are.

## Electron domains and shapes

| Domains | Domain geometry | Bonding domains | Nonbonding domains | Molecular shape | Bond angle | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Linear | 2 | 0 | Linear | $180°$ | $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{HCN}$ |
| 3 | Trigonal planar | 3 | 0 | Trigonal planar | $120°$ | $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{SO_3}$ |
| 3 | Trigonal planar | 2 | 1 | Bent (V-shaped) | $\sim 117°$ | $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$ |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 4 | 0 | Tetrahedral | $109.5°$ | $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 3 | 1 | Trigonal pyramidal | $107°$ | $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{PCl_3}$ |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 2 | 2 | Bent | $104.5°$ | $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{SCl_2}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 5 | 0 | Trigonal bipyramidal | $90°/120°$ | $\mathrm{PF_5}$, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 4 | 1 | Seesaw | $\sim 90°/120°$ | $\mathrm{SF_4}$, $\mathrm{TeCl_4}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 3 | 2 | T-shaped | $\sim 90°$ | $\mathrm{ClF_3}$, $\mathrm{BrF_3}$ |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 2 | 3 | Linear | $180°$ | $\mathrm{XeF_2}$, $\mathrm{I_3^-}$ |
| 6 | Octahedral | 6 | 0 | Octahedral | $90°$ | $\mathrm{SF_6}$, $\mathrm{MoF_6}$ |
| 6 | Octahedral | 5 | 1 | Square pyramidal | $\sim 90°$ | $\mathrm{BrF_5}$, $\mathrm{IF_5}$ |
| 6 | Octahedral | 4 | 2 | Square planar | $90°$ | $\mathrm{XeF_4}$, $\mathrm{PtCl_4^{2-}}$ |

Reading down the four-domain block shows the pattern in miniature: the domain geometry stays tetrahedral throughout while the shape changes from tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal to bent, and the bond angle falls from $109.5°$ to $107°$ to $104.5°$ as each lone pair is added.

## Molecular polarity

**Nonpolar molecules:**

1. Symmetrical shape — linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral and so on.
2. All surrounding atoms identical, as in $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ and $\mathrm{BF_3}$.

**Polar molecules:**

1. Asymmetrical shape — bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw and so on.
2. Surrounding atoms differ in electronegativity, as in $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and $\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}$.

$\mathrm{CH_4}$ is nonpolar: it is tetrahedral, and all the surrounding atoms are hydrogen. A symmetrical arrangement of identical bonds means the individual bond dipoles have nothing to add up to.

## Practice problems

**Predict the shape of $\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}$.**

- Lewis structure: $\mathrm{S}$ is central, with $6 + 3 \times 6 + 2 = 26$ electrons; $\mathrm{S}$ has 1 lone pair and 3 bonding pairs.
- Electron domains: 4, being 3 bonding plus 1 nonbonding, so the domain geometry is tetrahedral.
- From the table, 4 domains with 3 bonding and 1 nonbonding gives a **trigonal pyramidal** shape.

**A polarity example.** A square planar molecule with identical $\mathrm{F}$ atoms is symmetrical, so it is nonpolar.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **VSEPR theory** | A theory that predicts three-dimensional molecular shapes by minimising repulsion between electron domains, both bonding and nonbonding |
| **Electron domain** | A region of electron density around the central atom; a single, double or triple bond each counts as 1 domain, as does each lone pair |
| **Electron domain geometry** | The arrangement set by the total number of domains: 2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral, and so on |
| **Molecular shape** | The arrangement obtained by ignoring the lone pairs in the domain geometry |
| **Nonpolar molecule** | A molecule with a symmetrical shape and identical surrounding atoms |
| **Polar molecule** | A molecule with an asymmetrical shape whose surrounding atoms differ in electronegativity |

# 9.4 Hybridisation and Bonding Theories

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

VSEPR predicts the shape. Hybridisation explains how the central atom's orbitals arrange themselves to produce it.

## Hybrid orbitals

**Hybridisation** is the mixing of atomic orbitals (s, p, d) to form new hybrid orbitals with equal energy and specific geometries.

| Hybridisation | Atomic orbitals mixed | Electron domains | Geometry | Bond angle | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $sp$ | 1 s + 1 p | 2 | Linear | $180°$ | $\mathrm{BeF_2}$, $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$ (acetylene) |
| $sp^2$ | 1 s + 2 p | 3 | Trigonal planar | $120°$ | $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ (ethylene) |
| $sp^3$ | 1 s + 3 p | 4 | Tetrahedral | $109.5°$ | $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ |
| $sp^3d$ | 1 s + 3 p + 1 d | 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | $90°/120°$ | $\mathrm{PF_5}$, $\mathrm{SF_4}$, $\mathrm{BrF_3}$ |
| $sp^3d^2$ | 1 s + 3 p + 2 d | 6 | Octahedral | $90°$ | $\mathrm{SF_6}$, $\mathrm{XeF_4}$, $\mathrm{IF_5}$ |

**The shortcut: electron domains = number of hybrid orbitals.** So 5 domains means $sp^3d$. The superscripts in each label are just a count of how many orbitals went into the mix, and that count must equal the number of domains coming out — which is why the table can be reconstructed rather than memorised.

## Sigma and pi bonds

| Bond type | Formation | Strength | Rotation | Occurrence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sigma$ (sigma) | Head-on overlap of orbitals (s-s, s-p, p-p) | Strongest | Free | All single bonds; 1 per multiple bond |
| $\pi$ (pi) | Side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals | Weaker than $\sigma$ | Restricted | Double bonds (1 $\pi$), triple bonds (2 $\pi$) |

The rotation column is the practically useful one. A $\sigma$ bond's head-on overlap is unchanged when one end turns, so rotation is free; a $\pi$ bond's side-by-side overlap is destroyed by rotation, so double and triple bonds are locked rigid.

### Examples

**$\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ (ethylene):** the $\mathrm{C=C}$ double bond is 1 $\sigma$ from $sp^2$-$sp^2$ overlap plus 1 $\pi$ from p-p side overlap.

**$\mathrm{C_2H_2}$ (acetylene):** the $\mathrm{C \equiv C}$ triple bond is 1 $\sigma$ from $sp$-$sp$ overlap plus 2 $\pi$ from p-p side overlaps.

## Delocalisation and resonance

**Resonance structures** are multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule, as in $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ and $\mathrm{O_3}$.

$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ has 3 resonance structures, and its $\pi$ electrons are delocalised over the $\mathrm{N-O}$ bonds. Delocalisation is the reason the several drawn structures are needed: the $\pi$ electrons are not confined to one bond, so no single structure can place them correctly.

## Practice problems

**What is the hybridisation of the central atom in $\mathrm{CO_2}$?**

Linear geometry gives 2 electron domains, so the hybridisation is $sp$.

**And for a tetrahedral molecule?**

A tetrahedral shape gives 4 electron domains, so the hybridisation is $sp^3$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hybridisation** | The mixing of atomic orbitals (s, p, d) to form new hybrid orbitals with equal energy and specific geometries |
| **Sigma ($\sigma$) bond** | A bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals; the strongest bond type, with free rotation, found in all single bonds and once per multiple bond |
| **Pi ($\pi$) bond** | A bond formed by side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals; weaker than a sigma bond, with restricted rotation, found in double bonds (1) and triple bonds (2) |
| **Resonance structures** | Multiple valid Lewis structures for a molecule, arising because the $\pi$ electrons are delocalised |

# 9.5 Intermolecular and Intramolecular Forces

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

**Intramolecular forces** are the forces that exist inside molecules — only the covalent bond.

**Intermolecular forces** are the forces of attraction between neighbouring molecules.

The two prefixes are the whole distinction: *intra* is within one molecule, *inter* is between separate molecules. Breaking an intramolecular force means destroying the molecule; overcoming an intermolecular force only means separating molecules from one another.

## The three intermolecular forces

### London dispersion forces

A force of attraction between **induced dipoles**, present in **all molecular substances**.

Because they are induced rather than permanent, nothing about a molecule's structure is required for them to exist — which is why this is the one force every molecular substance has.

### Dipole-dipole forces

Attractions between the opposite charges of neighbouring dipoles.

Polar molecules have **permanent dipoles**. Whether a molecule is a permanent dipole depends on two things: whether it has polar bonds, and the geometry of the molecule. Both conditions are needed — polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel out, which is why molecular shape has to be settled before polarity can be decided.

### Hydrogen bonding

The extremely strong dipole-dipole force between the $\mathrm{H}$ atom of one molecule and the $\mathrm{N}$, $\mathrm{O}$ or $\mathrm{F}$ atoms of another molecule.

Hydrogen bonding is a special case of the dipole-dipole force rather than a separate mechanism, distinguished by how strong it is and by the restriction to those three partner atoms.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Intramolecular forces** | The forces that exist inside molecules (only the covalent bond) |
| **Intermolecular forces** | The forces of attraction between neighbouring molecules |
| **London dispersion forces** | A force of attraction between induced dipoles, present in all molecular substances |
| **Dipole-dipole forces** | Attractions between opposite charges of neighbouring dipoles |
| **Permanent dipole** | A polar molecule; whether a molecule is one depends on whether it has polar bonds and on the geometry of the molecule |
| **Hydrogen bonding** | The extremely strong dipole-dipole force between the $\mathrm{H}$ atom of one molecule and the $\mathrm{N}$, $\mathrm{O}$ or $\mathrm{F}$ atoms of another |

## 6.7 Many-Electron Atoms

**Orbitals and Their Energy:**

- One-electron atoms:
  - All subshells with the same principal quantum number are degenerate
    - Degenerate = same energy for every electron within that subshell
- Many-electron atom:
  - Contains electron-electron repulsion = different energies
    - Energy order: Typically, ns<np<nd<nf

Note: Exceptions exist, e.g., 4s is lower in energy than 3d for transition metals.

  - Yet orbitals within the same subshell are degenerate
    - E.g. ${P}_{x}={P}_{y}={P}_{z}$
  - The energy of different principal levels may overlap.
    - E.g. Energy for 4s < 3d

**Aufbau Principle**

- Electrons occupy the orbital of the lowest energy first
- Orbitals of the same sublevel always have the same energy
- On the same principal energy level: s<p<d<f
- 1s<2s<2p<3s<3p<4s<3d<4p<5s<4d<5p<6s<4f<5d<6p<7s>5f<6d<7p

**Pauli Exclusion Principle:**

- An atomic orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons and they must have the opposite spin
  - Only when two electrons of opposite spin occupy an electron, it is paired
- Spin is a property of electrons
  - Spin clockwise/counterclockwise, the arrow pointing up is clockwise, pointing down is counterclockwise.

**6.8+6.9 Electron Configurations and the Periodic Table:**

**Orbital Diagram:**

- Box: one orbital
- Half Arrow: one electron
- Direction: the relative spin of the electron

**Electron Configuration:**

$$1{s}^{2}2{s}^{1}$$

- Coefficient: energy level
- Letter: type of orbital
- Superscript: number of electrons in that sublevel/subshell

**Hund’s Rule:**

- For degenerate orbitals, electrons will occupy empty orbitals with parallel spins before pairing up in the same orbital
- This meant that you fill out all the orbitals with arrows pointing in the same direction (or the maximum number of orbitals you may fill) before you start pairing them as two electrons in one orbital
- Orbitals are filled in order of increasing energy
- A maximum of two electrons are in each orbital

**Abbreviated Electron Configurations:**

- Aka: Condensed electron Configurations / Noble gas notation
- To substitute the core electrons with the previous noble gas (Or He as an exception) presented
- Represented in its chemical symbol in brackets
- E.g.: C: $1{s}^{2}2{s}^{2}2{p}^{4}$ can be written in:
  - $\left[ He \right] 2{s}^{2}2{p}^{4}$, as He is the previous noble gas while $2{s}^{2}2{p}^{4}$ are retained. *Even if the current element is a noble gas, you should still chose the previous noble gas to replace its core electrons. Eg. Ne=$\left[ He \right] 2{s}^{2}2{p}^{6}$

**Valence Electrons:**

- Core electrons: Inner Shell Electrons
  - This is basically the electron configuration for the noble gas core
  - E.g. $1{s}^{2}$ in C
- Outer shell electrons: electrons after the noble gas core
  - E.g. $2{s}^{2}2{p}^{4}$ in C
- Valence Electrons: Electrons responsible for chemical bonding and chemical behavior
  - For elements with an atomic number of 30 or less, the valence electrons are generally those in the outermost shell. (Note: for transition metals like Zn (atomic number 30), the d-electrons may also be considered valence electrons depending on context)
    - E.g. $2{s}^{2}2{p}^{4}$ in C
  - For transition elements:
    - Usually, it only includes the outermost electrons (in the biggest shell)
    - E.g. Cu = [Ar] $4{s}^{1} 3{d}^{10}$
      - Because $4{s}^{1}$ it is located in the outermost shell, it is the valence electron for this element
    - This rule will be more complicated when encountering deeper chemistry, but remember it like this just now

**Tips in Writing the Electron configuration of the element:**

- Write down [Noble Gas] ns np
- Add $(n-2){f}^{14}$if it is placed after the f block
- Add $(n-1)$ ${d}^{10}$ if the element is placed after the d block

**Tips when given the electron configuration**

- When given the full configuration, count up the electrons and locate the element to its atomic number (when it is a neutral atom)
- When given a condensed configuration, first locate the noble gas, and then add up the number of electrons. Then with the number of electrons, count up the same number after the noble gas.

**Electron Configurations of the Excited State:**

- Ground State: the most stable organization of electrons in its lowest possible energy
  - E.g. F : $1{s}^{2} 2{s}^{2}2{p}^{5}$
- Excited State: shows one or more electrons in a higher energy level
  - E.g. F : $1{s}^{2} 2{s}^{2}2{p}^{4} 3{s}^{1}$
- Tips for identifying the excited state:
- Make sure that the number of electrons corresponds to the atomic number of the element
- Remove the answer choice of ground choice
- Make sure that all the orbitals are correctly filled

**Electron Configuration for Ions**

- Atoms gain/lose electrons to achieve a stable noble gas configuration
  - usually an octet
- Metal Elements tend to lose electrons -> Form Cations
  - E.g. ${Mg}^{2+ }=\left[ Ne \right]$
- Non-metal elements tend to gain electrons -> Form Anions
  - E.g. ${Cl}^{- }=\left[ Ar \right]$
- Transition metals will lose outmost shell electron first, then lose the inner ones
  - E.g. ${Fe}^{2+ }=\left[ Ar \right]3{d}^{6}$

**Exceptional Electron Configurations**

- Cr (24) -> expected -> $\left[ Ar \right]4{s}^{2} 3{d}^{4}$
  - Actual -> $\left[ Ar \right]4{s}^{1} 3{d}^{5}$
- Mo (42) -> expected -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{2} 4{d}^{4}$
  - Actual ->$\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{1} 4{d}^{5}$
- Ru (44) -> expected -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{2} 4{d}^{6}$
  - Actual -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{1} 4{d}^{7}$
- Cu (29) -> expected -> $\left[ Ar \right]4{s}^{2} 3{d}^{9}$
  - Actual -> $\left[ Ar \right]4{s}^{1} 3{d}^{10}$
- Ag (47) -> expected -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{2} 4{d}^{9}$
  - Actual ->$\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{1} 4{d}^{10}$
- Au (79) -> expected -> $\left[ Xe \right]6{s}^{2} 4{f}^{14}5{d}^{9}$
  - Actual -> $\left[ Xe \right]6{s}^{1} 4{f}^{14}5{d}^{10}$
- Pd (46) -> expected -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{2}4{d}^{8}$
  - Actual -> $\left[ Kr \right]4{d}^{10}$
- Nb (48) ->expected -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{2} 4{d}^{3}$
  - Actual -> $\left[ Kr \right]5{s}^{1} 4{d}^{4}$
- General rules for the patterns:
  - When encountering situations of near half-filled/filled configurations
    - Move one s orbital electron to the higher energy orbital
    - An exception occurs in Pd, where both electrons in the s orbital would move to higher-energy levels.

**Electron Configuration and Periodic Table:**

- S block + p block = main group elements / representative elements
- D block = transition elements
- F block = inner transition elements
  - Aka : Lanthanides (4f) /actinides (5f)

Accepted value: the “true” value of the measurement

For series of measurements, the closer they come to each other, the more precise.

**4.Error and uncertainty**

Error = experimental value – accepted value

Error can be a negative value

Poor accuracy in measurements is usually associated with a systematic error.

Systematic errors are **always biased in the same direction**.

common sources:

zero error, badly made instruments, improper procedures or theories...

Systematic errors **cannot be reduced by repetition.**

**Random uncertainty**

**Poor precision in measurements is associated with random uncertainty.**

Error associated with estimating the last digit of a reading is called random uncertainty. Usually caused by instrument limits.

Can sometimes be higher than true value sometimes lower.

**Repeating the measurement** **for multiple** **times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random uncertainty.**

For the instrument with a **scale,** the uncertainty equal to half of the scale graduations. (Ruler, thermometer…)

Eg. The uncertainty of a 20cm ruler is 0.05cm

For an instrument with a **digital display,** the uncertainty is ±1 in the last decimal place of the reading, or in other words, the least count.

**Absolute uncertainty**

Keep only 1 sf for abs uncertainty.

eg. 1.00 ±0.01g the abs uncertainty is 0.01

percentage uncertainty=abs uncertainty/true value

# S1F-2 Chapter 7 Periodic Properties of the Elements

## Chapter 7 Periodic Properties of the Elements

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Chemistry H review guide (PA). Writers: Cherie 9-10, Jazzlynne 9-11. Editor: Kenny 9-6. Range: Chp 6, Chp 1.4-1.6, Lab, Chp 7.1-7.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**Scope:**

## 7.1 Development of Periodic Table

## 7.2 Effective Nuclear Charge

## 7.3 Sizes of Atoms and Ions

## 7.1 Development of the Periodic Table

**Time Table of Events**

- 1790: Antoine Lavoisier made a list of 23 elements
- 1860: A method for determining atomic mass was being agreed upon
- 1964: John Newland proposed to arrange the elements with increasing atomic mass
  - Concluded that their properties repeated every 8th element
  - This type of pattern is named periodic, because it repeats in a specific manner
  - Also (octave)
- 1869: Dmitri Mendeleev and Lothar Meyer demonstrated the connection between atomic mass and elemental properties
  - Mendeleev -> published earlier + more specific -> more famous
- 1870s: 70 known elements
- 1913: Henry Moseley arranged with atomic number
  - This is the creation of the modern Periodic Table
  - A clear periodic pattern of properties arranged

**Mendeleev’s achievements:**

- Noticed that when elements are organized with increasing atomic mass -> repetition / periodic pattern in chemical and physical properties
  - Showed that they repeated from row to row of the table
  - In the same vertical columns -> similar properties
- He correctly predicted the existence and properties of undiscovered elements
- But since he didn’t find all the elements
  - Left some blank spaces in the periodic table
  - With this, he can predict the properties of Scandium, Gallium, and Germanium that were previously undiscovered
    - He named them eka-silicon as they are being categorized in the same group with silicon (with the same properties)
    - Anything with the prefix eka- indicates that it shares similar properties and belongs to the group whose element serves as the root.
- He corrected the atomic mass of elements
  - E.g., Be, In, U, Os, Ir, Pt, Y, and Ti
- To fit in with the pattern of chemical properties
  - He sometimes broke the pattern of the increasing atomic mass when arranging
  - E.g., No.52 (127.6 mass) arranged before No.53 (126.9045)

**Verification of his Prediction: Gallium**

- Mendeleev predicted an aluminum-like element
  - Atomic weight = 68, density=5.9
- In 1875, A French chemist discovered a new element
  - Atomic weight = 69.9, density of 4.7
  - Everything is consistent with what Mendeleev predicted, except the density
- Mendeleev wrote a letter stating that the density is being mismeasured
  - And after a second experiment, it is confirmed that the density is 5.94

**7.2 Effective Nuclear Charge:**

**In a many-electron atom:**

- Electron [1] attracted to nucleus [2] repelled by other electrons
- Both factors affect the nuclear charge an electron receives
- Valence electrons experience less attraction to the nucleus

Because they receive a repulsion of core electrons

- Shielding effect: Repelling effect inner electrons have on valence electrons -> decrease in the amount of attraction felt by the valence electrons from the nuclear charge
- Effective Nuclear charge:

Charged felt by the valence electrons of an atom after the number of shielding electrons that surround the nucleus is taken into account

In Other words:

$${Z}_{\text{ eff }}=Z-S$$

Where:

${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ Is the effective nuclear Charge

Z is the nuclear charge (number of protons).

S is the shielding constant (near to the number of core electrons).

Z is decided by the number of protons only

To predict the Shielding Constant: *Not tested*

$$S\approx (\# \text{ inner } \text{ electrons })\times 0.85+(\#\text{ same }-\text{ shell } \text{ electrons })\times 0.35$$

${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$in the outermost electrons is smaller than inner electrons due to the screening of the inner electrons

Inner electrons have a greater impact on screening than outer electrons.

**Patterns of** ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$

- Across a period, S stays the same as they have the same core electrons, but Z will gradually increase with increasing proton.
- increasing ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ (significantly)
- Down a group, the Z increases significantly as the number of protons increases, but S increases almost as much as there will be one more full inner shell of electrons being added
- The more diffuse core electron is less able to screen the valence electrons from the nuclear charge
- The inner electron shells become larger with increasing principal quantum number n -> more spread out from the nucleus -> less effective at shielding
- ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ increases slightly down a group

This pattern is an exception for d and f-block elements

D block ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ increases more notably

F block ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ increases even more

For the same principal energy level:

${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ : S > P > D > F

because s-orbital’s greater electron density near the nucleus = less shielding from other inner electrons.

**7.3 Sizes of Atoms and Ions:**

**Sizes** **of Atoms:**

Bonding Atomic radius: one-half of the distance between covalently bonded nuclei

Atomic Radius (measured in pm)

**Atomic Radius Patterns:**

Move down a group: more principal energy levels -> greater repulsion force between electrons -> atomic radius larger

Larger orbitals -> valence electrons are further away from the nucleus

Although ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$ decreases slightly within a group from left to right, the fact that the electrons are in a higher principal quantum shell outweighs the slight pull of ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$

Move left to right in a period -> gain more protons -> ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$increase -> stronger pull on electrons with the same principal energy level -> atomic radius decreases.

**Ionic Radius Patterns:**

- Cations (positively charged ions) are smaller than parent atoms
- Loss of outer electron
- Increased effective nuclear charge
- Same nuclear charge (# of protons) but fewer electrons
- Reduced electron-electron repulsion
- Anions (negatively charged ions) are larger than parent ions
- Added electrons (but no change in principal quantum number)
- Increased electron-electron repulsion
- More electrons in the same outer shell
- Decreased effective nuclear charge per electron
- Same nuclear charge (#of protons) but more electrons

**Isoelectronic Series:**

Atoms with the same number of electrons but different nuclear charges

Those with the greatest nuclear charge (# of protons) have the smallest atomic radius. This changes dramatically

E.g. ${O}^{2-}$ and ${F}^{-}$ both have the same number of electrons, but since O has 8 protons and F has 9 protons, O is a larger atom compared to F

**Exceptions:**

Transition metals change irregularly:

They have variable Oxidation states (they may have many changes instead of only having one or two charges in the main group elements

Many are catalytic, readily accepting or donating electrons to provide a reactive surface for reactions.

For multiple charges in the Same Element:

Higher charge = smaller ion

E.g. ${Fe}^{2+}\left( 78pm \right)>{Fe}^{3+}\left( 65pm \right)$

Because higher ${Z}_{\text{ eff }}$pulls electrons closer

**Coulomb’s law: *probably not tested***

$$F=k \frac{{Q}_{1}∙{Q}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}$$

Where:

F= Force (Newtons)

k= Coulomb’s constant = $9∙{10}^{9}N∙{m}^{2}/{C}^{2}$

R = distance between them (meters)

${Q}_{1}$and${Q}_{2}$ = charges of the two particles (Coulombs)

Measures the electrostatic force between two charged particles

Inside Atoms, it includes:

[1] Electron-Nucleus attraction

[2] Electron-Electron repulsion

[3] Proton-Proton repulsion

The magnitude and direction of the force

# S2M-1 Semester 2 Midterm review: Chapter 7.4-8.7

## Semester 2 Midterm review: Chapter 7.4-8.7

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Midterm Chemistry H review guide (PA). Writers: Leyi Lian 9-5, Kelvin Chen 9-2. Editor: Nicky Yang 9-11. Range: Chapter 7.4-8.7. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**7-4 Ionization Energy**

-Ionization Energy: Amount of energy required to remove an electron (valence first) from the ground state of a gaseous atom or ion.

=GASEOUS: to exclude intermolecular forces

=REQUIRED: Always positive

=First Ionization Energy (IE1): Energy required to remove the first valence electron

Unit: J/atom, kJ/mol

Reactant Side Li(g)Li(g)++e- Product

**Trend**

-Down a Group:

=1) Zeff is the same

=2) Valence electrons farther from the nucleus (see atomic radius 7-3 for detail, shielding effect)

=3) Less energy required—Decrease

-Across a Row (Left to Right):

=1) Zeff increases with more protons in the nucleus

=2) Harder to remove electron—Increase

-First to Second Ionization Energy (same for second to third, third to fourth, etc.):

=1) Removing an electron from a more positively charged ion

=2) Requires more energy to remove each successive electron—Increase

=When all valence electrons have been removed, ionization energy takes a quantum leap to break through another shell

**Discontinuities**

1)2A to 3A—Decrease

2A [ns2] 3A [ns2 np1]

-Electron removed from p-orbital rather than s-orbital

=(p-orbital) At a higher energy level and less attracted to the nucleus

2)5A to 6A—Decrease

5A [ns2 np3] 6A [ns2 np4]

**Please note that the PA materials are created by students and are only materials for reference.**

**Should any part of the materials differ from the content in class, please make sure to follow the content in class.**

-Electron removed from a doubly occupied orbital

=Repulsion from the other electron helps in its removal

**7-5 Electron Affinity and Electronegativity**

**Electron Affinity**

-Electron Affinity: Energy change accompanying addition of electrons to a gaseous atom

=CHANGE: ‘+’: Absorb; ‘-’: Release

-The more negative the electron affinity, the greater the attraction to the added electron

Ne(g)+eNe-(g)

**Trend**

-Down a Group:

=1) Zeff is the same

=2) Greater atomic radius

=3) Harder to add electron—More positive

-Across a Row:

=1) Zeff increases, higher attraction

=2) Releases energy—More negative/Exothermic

**Discontinuities**

1)1A to 2A—Less Negative

1A [ns1] 2A [ns2]

-For 2A, the added electron must go in the p-orbital (farther from the nucleus and requires more energy)

=Electron feels repulsion from s-orbital electrons

2)4A to 5A—Less Negative

4A [ns2 np2] 5A [ns2 np3]

-5A has no empty orbitals, so the extra electron must go into an occupied orbital

=Repulsion exists, more energy required

**Electronegativity (EN)**

-Electronegativity: The ability of an atom to attract bonding electrons when the atom is in a compound

=Using the Pauling Scale

**Trend**

-Down a Group:

=1) Zeff is the same

=2) Valence shell is less strongly held by the nucleus (increasing shielding effect)

=3) Harder to attract electrons—Decrease

-Across a Row (for representative elements):

=1) Zeff increases, greater attraction

=2) Easier to attract electrons—Increase

-Highest (Strong ability to gain): F

-Lowest (Strong ability to lose): Fr

**7-6 Metal, Nonmetals, and Metalloids**

-Metals tend to form cations(+)

-Nonmetals tend to form anions(-)

Exceptions: Hydrogen is a nonmetal but can form both cation and anion

**Metals**

-Lustrous—Shine

-Malleable: Can be forced into any shape

-Ductile: Can be drawn into wires

-Good conductors of heat and electricity

-Mostly solid at room temperature (25 degrees Celsius)

=Exception: Mercury Hg(L)

-Compounds formed between metals and nonmetals tend to be ionic

=Due to a great difference in EN (Metals usually lower and nonmetals higher)

-Metal oxides tend to be basic

**Nonmentals**

-Dull, brittle (for those in the solid state) substances

-Poor conductors of heat and electricity

-odorless, colorless gas (for those in the gas state), except F and Cl

-Tend to gain electrons in reactions with metals to acquire noble gas configurations

-Molecular Compound: A substance containing only nonmetals and forming covalent bonds

-Most nonmetal oxides are acidic

**Metalloids**

-Under some conditions behave as metal, some as nonmetal

=e.g., Si looks shiny, has metallic luster, acts as a semiconductor, has high hardness, and has a relatively high melting point

-B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po

**Summary**

**8-1 Lewis Symbol and Octet Rule**

-Chemical Bond: The electrostatic (positive-negative) attraction force that holds two atoms together

=Ionic Bond: Attraction between cations and anions—Metal and Nonmetal

=Covalent Bond: Attraction between the nucleus and shared electrons—Nonmetal and Nonmetal

=Metallic Bond: Attraction between metal cations and delocalized electrons (shared among more than 2 atoms in a molecule)—Metal and Metal

-The formation of a chemical bond helps decrease chemical potential energy

-Octet Rule: All elements tend to have electron configurations consisting of 8 electrons in the outermost shell—Stable Octet

=Except H, He

-Lewis Symbols: Element’s chemical symbol + a dot to represent each valence electron

=First on four sides, then get paired

**8-2 Ionic Bonding**

**Cation**

-Elements with low EN tend to form positive ions by losing electrons (metals, H)

e.g., Na ([Ne] 3s1) Na+ ([He]2s2 2p6)

-For representative elements

- metals: the charge of its ion = number of valence electrons (group number)
- nonmetals: the charge of its ion = number of valence electrons (group number) - 8

-For transition elements, they form various ions with different charges, because d-orbitals and f-orbitals are involved

=2+ and 3+ are common (e.g., Cr, Fe)

-For elements 1B to 4A in period 4 to 6, they form pseudo-noble gas notation, which is relatively stable

=e.g., Pb ([Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 6p2), if electrons from 6p orbital are lost, it will have a 2+ charge; if from 6p and 6s orbitals are lost, it will have a 4+ charge

**Anion**

-Elements with high EN tend to form anions by gaining electrons (nonmetals)

e.g., Cl ([Ne] 3s2 3p5)Cl-([Ne] 3s2 3p6)

-For nonmetal, the charge = difference between its valence electrons and 8

**Naming Ions**

-Monatomic ions: Consist of a single atom with a positive or negative charge resulting from the loss or gain of 1 or more valence electrons

-Cations: Names as elements, followed by the word “ion” or “cation”

e.g., Na+, Sodium ion (or cation)

-Anions: Start with the stem of the element name and end in -ide

e.g., F-, Fluoride

-Metals that form more than 1 ion (Transition metals): Place a Roman numeral in parentheses

e.g., Fe2+, Iron (II) Ion

Exceptions: Zn2+ Zinc Ion, Ag+ Silver Ion (they have only 1 common charge)

**Naming Ionic Compounds**

-Ionic Compounds are electically neutralCharges of cation+anion must balance

-Exist as collections of positively and negatively charged ions arranged in a repeating pattern

AXBY

-Composed of 2 elements: A-metal, B-nonmetal

-x,y: Subscripts needed to balance the charge (crisscriss method, but remember to simplify and leave the smallest ratio)

=Formula Unit: The lowest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound

-Place cation first, then anion

-If the metallic element has more than one common ionic charge, a Roman numeral must be included

e.g., CuOCopper (II) Oxide

**Properties**

-High melting point/boiling point and hardness

=+,- have high attraction, and are difficult to break bonds

-Brittle: Ordered crystal lattice structure

=When a force is exerted, layers shift, and the same charges will be in corresponding positions and repel each other

-Solid does not conduct electricity

=Ions are in a fixed position

-Molten or aqueous solutions of ionic conductors can conduct

=Free-moving ions, and for aqueous solutions, water binds to the ions, and compounds dissolve

-Ionic crystals vary in shape due to size and the relative numbers of ions bonded

-Lattice Energy: Energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions

NaCl(s)Na+(g)+Cl-(g)

-The strength of the ionic bond

-Greater attraction force between cations and anions, greater lattice energy (more positive)

-Larger Charges: Greater attractionMore positive lattice energy

-Smaller Sizes (Distance): Greater attractionMore positive lattice energy

**8-3** **Covalent Bonding**

**What is a Covalent Bond**

-Covalent Bond is the electrostatic force between sharing electrons and the nucleus

-Formed when both atoms have high EN (Electron Negativity)

-Sharing of electrons between atoms

**Single Covalent Bonds**

-A single covalent bond is when 2 atoms share only 1 pair of electrons

-AKA: Single bond

-E.g. F2 Cl2 H2O

-Group 4 elements can form 4 single bonds, Group 5 elements can form 3 single bonds, Group 6 elements can form 2 single bonds, Group 7 elements can form only 1 single bond.

**Sigma (σ) Bonds**

-A sigma bond is formed when 2 s or p orbitals perform head-on overlap

-All single bonds are sigma bonds

-Sigma bonds are free to rotate on the bond axis

-Can be formed between s-s, s-p, or p-p orbitals

**Pi (π) Bonds**

-Pi bond is formed between 2 parallel p orbitals

-In a pi bond, the electrons tend to be found on sausage shaped regions above and below the bond axis

-Pi bond overlaps less than sigma bond, so pi bonds tend to be weaker

-A pi bond can only form if a sigma bond already exists between the 2 atoms

-Pi bond is not free to rotate

**Multiple Covalent Bonds**

-More than one pair of electron is shared between 2 atoms

-Double bond: 2 pairs of electrons are shared

-Triple bond: 3 pairs of electrons are shared

-Only one sigma can be formed between 2 atoms

-Bond association energy is the energy required to break the bond between 2 covalently bonded atoms

-Energy is released when chemical bonds are formed

-Bond dissociation energy indicates the strength of a chemical bond.

-Bond length has an inverse relationship with the bond dissociation energy, and has direct relationship with the number of shared electrons.

-Atoms of form longer bonds when the atoms are bigger in size

**Summary**

**Compare Molecular and Ionic Compounds**

- Representative Unit

Molecular compound (joined by covalent bonds): Molecule

Ionic compound: Formula unit

-Formula unit is lowest whole number ratio of ions in an ionic compound

- Melting Point

-Molecular compounds tend to have relatively lower melting and boiling points than ionic compounds

-Most molecular compounds are gases or liquid at room temperature

- How to classify Ionic or Molecular compound
- Metal+Nonmetal=ionic compound
- Nonmetal+Nonmetal=Molecular compound

**Polyatomic ions**

- Polyatomic ions

-Composed of more than one atom

-Behaves as a unit and carry charge

Rules for naming

- End with suffix -ate for ions with more oxygen atoms

End with suffix -ite for ions with less oxygen atoms

Ex. SO32- Sulfite SO42- Sulfate

- Add prefix -per and suffix -ate for ions with the greatest number of oxygen atoms

Add prefix -hypo and suffix -ite for ions with fewest number of oxygen atoms

Ex. ClO4- ClO3 ClO2- ClO- Called perchlorate, chlorate, chlorite, and hypochlorite respectively

- Add hydrogen before the naming of polyatomic ion if hydrogen is added in the compound

Named like this when the final compound still has charge (Or else it would be another rule)

Ex. CO32 -Carbonate HCO3 - Hydrogen Carbonate (Also called Bicarbonate)

PO43- Phosphate HPO42- Hydrogen phosphate H2PO4- Dihydrogen phosphate

- Compounds you just got to remember (There is absolute no rules for these)

Acetate: C2H3O2- Carbonate:CO32- Cyanide:CN- Ammonium:NH4+

Hydroxide: OH- Peroxide ion: O22- Hydronium ion: H3O+ Permanganate: MnO4-

- Compounds with polyatomic ions

-Whenever more than 1 polyatomic ion is needed to balance the charges in an ionic compound, use parentheses to set oof the polyatomic ion in the formula

Ex. Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)2

- Naming compounds with polyatomic ions

-Write Cation before Anion

NaClO

Na+ Sodium ion ClO- hypochlorite ion

NaClO= Sodium hypochlorite

**Naming and writing formulas for Molecular Compounds**

- Binary Molecular compounds

AxBy where A and B are both nonmetals

-Write the names of the elements in the order listed in the formula

-Use prefixes appropriately to indicate the number of each kind of atom

-End the name of the second element with the suffix -ide

-If just one atom of the first element is in the formula, omit the prefix mono- for that element. -Vowel at the end of a prefix is sometimes dropped when the name of the element begins with a vowel

Prefix table:

| Prefix | Number |
|---|---|
| Mono- | 1 |
| Di- | 2 |
| Tri- | 3 |
| Tetra- | 4 |
| Penta- | 5 |
| Hexa- | 6 |
| Hepta- | 7 |
| Octa- | 8 |
| Nona- | 9 |
| Deca- | 10 |

Examples: CO2 Carbon dioxide P2O5 Diphosphorus pentoxide

Exceptions: H2O water NH3 Ammonia CH4 Methane

There are different rules for organic compounds (Compounds that includes carbon and hydrogen only).

**Naming and writing formulas for acids and bases**

- Names and Formulas of Acids

-Acid is a compound that contains one or more hydrogen atoms and produces hydrogen ions when dissolved in water.

Ex. HCl(g) ---> Cl-(aq) +H+(aq）

Naming Acids (rules)

- Anion: ___ide ---> acid: Hydro____ic acid

Ex. Cl- (chloride) --> HCl (hydrochloric acid)

- Anion: ____ate ---> acid:___ic acid

Ex. ClO3- (Chlorate) ---> HClO3 (chloric acid)

- Anion: _____ite ---> acid: _____ous acid

Ex. SO32- (Sulfite) ----> H2SO3 (sulfurous acid)

-No need for clarifying the amount of hydrogen needed when naming acids

-Special case for phosphorus, where phosphite or phosphate becomes phosphorous acid and phosphoric acid (not phosphous or phosphic)

- Names and Formulas of Bases

-A base is a compound that produces hydroxide ions when dissolved in water (generally is an ionic compound)

NaOH ---> Na+ + OH-

Rules:

-The name of the cation is followed by the name of the anion

Ex. Al(OH)3 Aluminum Hydroxide

**8-4** **Bond Polarity and Electronegativity (EN)**

- **Electronegativity**

-Electronegativity is defined as the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract electrons to itself

-American scientist Linus Pauling developed first and most widely used EN scale which is called the Pauling scale.

-Pauling scale is a relative scale running from 0.7(Fr) to 3.98(F) and is a dimensionless quantity

-In general, EN values decrease from top to bottom, and increase from left to right

- **Polarity of the Bond**

-Polarity refers to a separation of positive and negative charge.

-In a nonpolar bond, the bonding electrons are shared equally

-In a polar bond, electrons are shared unequally

-In a compound, the atom with a lower EN is called the partially positive end, and the atom with a higher EN is called a partially negative end

-You can express a polar bond in 2 ways

-The symbol in the second picture is lower case delta (δ) which expresses H as the partially positive charge and Cl as the partially negative charge

-How to determine the type of bond if you know the difference of the electronegativity

**8-5 Drawing Lewis Structures**

Molecular formula: Shows all the numbers of atoms in one molecule

Lewis Structure: Uses letter symbols and bonds to show relative position of atoms

Structural formula: Similar to Lewis structure but unpaired electrons are omitted

**Guide to writing Lewis structures**

**Formal Charge** **(CHECK AFTER DRAWING ONLY IF CENTRAL IS PERIOD 3 OR AFTER)**

-Formal charge= v.e.-(bonding electrons/2 + non-bonding electrons)

-First write the symbol, then the number (ex. -1/+2)

-The sum of the formal charges of the atoms should be equal to the overall charge of the compound

-The best Lewis Structure is the one with the fewest formal charges, and also puts the negative charge on the atom that has the largest EN

Ex. The last Lewis structure is the best because it has formal charge closer to 0 for each atom, and places the negative charge on the atom that has the largest EN which is oxygen

## 8.6 Resonance Structure

-Resonance is a condition that occurs when more than one valid Lewis structure can be written for a molecule or ion.

-Differ only in the position of electron pairs, not the Atom’s position

-All of these are the resonance structure of Nitrate, so during a test, you need to draw all 3 and connect them with arrows like in the picture above

-The actual structure of the molecule is a blend of all its resonance structures, which is called resonance hybrid

-In the resonance hybrid of a Nitrate ion (the example above), a delocalized pi bond is formed because all the bonds should have the same length and bond disassociation energy (All of the bonds between nitrogen and oxygen are the same, they are all stronger than a single bond, weaker than a double bond)

-This is actually how you draw a Nitrate ion with a dashed line for the delocalized pi bonds between Nitrogen and Oxygen and **DO NOT DRAW THIS ON THE EXAM.** This is only here for a better understanding.

-Another example is Benzene (C6H6)

-It has 2 resonance structure

-And below are the 2 ways of drawing the resonance hybrid for Benzene

## 8.7 Exceptions to the Octet Rule

**-Odd number of electron**

Ex. Lewis structure for NO

-Nitrogen and oxygen both have a formal charge of 0, so this is the best Lewis structure

-examples: NO, NO2, etc

**-Less than an octet**

Ex. Boron trifluoride

-For compounds that has less than 8 electrons for the central atom, it can easily combine with other compounds, forming a coordinate covalent bond

-Coordinate Covalent Bond is formed when both of the shared electrons are donate by the same atoms (Usually represented by an arrow)

Example of coordinate covalent bond

-One pair of electrons is completely donated by oxygen, so it is a coordinate covalent bond

**-More than eight valence electron (expanded octet)**

-An expanded octet can be explained by considering the d orbitals that occurs in the energy level of elements in 3rd period or higher

-Can only appear for elements after or on the third period

Ex. PCl5
