## Chapter 1

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 1 Final Chemistry S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Jessica 9-11. Editor: Olivia 9-11. Range: chp 6+1+7.1-7.3. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

**1. Rules for Rounding Numbers (Only for lab results)**

-If the number right next to the last sig. fig. is less than 5, don’ t change the last significant figure.

-If the number right next to the last sig. fig. is greater than 5, round up the last significant figure

-If the number right next to the last sig. fig. is equal to 5 and is followed by a non-zero, round up the last significant figure

-If the number right next to the last sig. fig. is equal to 5 and is not followed by a zero/nothing, look at the last significant figure

（四舍五入）

**significant digits**: valid/reliable digits in a measurement (include estimated digit

**-estimated/uncertain digit**: Last digit in a measurement

-Exact numbers have an infinite number of significant digits (e.g. constant：2)

-0.000034 = 2 significant digits

-0.0002500 = 4 significant digits

-190000 = 2 / 2-6significant digits

**Addition or Subtraction**- smallest number of decimal places.

**Multiplication and Division**-smallest number of significant figures

**2. Accuracy and precision**

-Accuracy: how close to truth value (Accepted value)

-Precision: the repeatability of the measurement using a given instrument (集中)

**3. Error**

-Error = experimental value – accepted value

-

**1) Systematic error**

- one direction low accuracy, can’t be reduce by repeating

-mis-calibrated device/wrong measuring technique

-e.g.: Reaction time, zero error

**2) Random errors**

-both direction, low precision, can be reduce by repeating

- **Least count:** smallest division that is marked

- **ILE** (Instrument limit of error): digital=least count, Analogue= ½ of least count

**(Measured value ± uncertainty) unit**

-Uncertainty: 1 sf

-Measured value’s last sf is in the same place as the uncertainty.

-Measured value and uncertainty have same power of ten

**Absolute uncertainty:** △x, size of error and units

**Precent uncertainty:** △x/x ×100% (keep have 1-2sf)

**Error:** Measured value-expected value

**Precent error:** |error|/ expected value (may have 1-2sf)

**Conversion Factors**

-a ratio of equivalent measurements

-have an unlimited number of significant figures and do not affect the rounding of a calculated answer

**4. Representing Data (Brief)**

Lab report

-Variables (independent variable, dependent variable, controlled variable)

-Cations: valence electron removed=repulsions between electrons are reduced=atoms become smaller

-Anions: valence electron added=more repulsions=atom size increases

-isoelectronic series: same number of electrons, ionic size decreases with an increasing

nuclear charge

# S2M-1 Part 1: Periodic Properties (Sections 7.4–7.6)

## Part 1: Periodic Properties (Sections 7.4–7.6)

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Midterm Chemistry S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 9-4. Editor: Justin Lee 9-4. Range: 7.4-8.7. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 7.4 Ionization Energy

**Definition**: Energy required to remove one electron from an atom in a gaseous state

Successive ionization energy increases because as more electrons are removed, electron-pair repulsions are reduced, so the attraction force between the electrons and the nucleus is stronger. **Once an atom loses all its valence electrons, there is a big jump to the next IE**

**Periodic trends:**

- Down a group (Top Bottom): Decreases
  - Atomic size increasesvalence electrons are farther from the nucleusshielding effect from inner electrons makes the attraction force weaker easier to remove an electron
- Across a period (Left Right): Increases
  - Nuclear charge (number of protons) increase but electrons are added to the same valence shellnucleus pulls electrons more stronglyharder to remove an electron

Exceptions: Groups 2A ↔ 3A: The electron being removed is from a higher-energy orbital.

Groups 5A ↔ 6A: Electron-electron repulsion in a paired orbital.

## 7.5 Electron Affinity & Electronegativity

**Electron affinity**

**Definition**: energy change that occurs when it gains an electron

- Negative electron affinity: the process is exothermic
- Positive electron affinity: the process is endothermic

**Periodic trends**

- Down a group (Top Bottom): Becomes more positive
  - Larger atomic size weaker attraction for the incoming electronendothermic
- Across a period (Left Right): Becomes more negative
  - Increasing nuclear charge pulls the added electron more stronglyexothermic

Exceptions: Group 2A: the extra electron must go in the p orbital, more energy required

Group 5A: adding an electron to a half-filled p orbital would cause repulsion, more energy required

**Electronegativity**

**Definition**: the ability of an atom to attract electrons when the atom is in a compound

- Measured through the Pauling Scale, running from around 0.7(Fr) to 3.98(F)

**Periodic trends**

- Down a group (Top Bottom): Decrease
  - Number of electron shells increasethe valence shell are getting less strongly held by the nucleusharder for the atom to attract electrons
- Across a period (Left Right): Increase
  - Proton number increasesthe attraction from the nucleus is getting greatereasier for the atom to attract electrons

**Noble gases do not have electronegativity values because they do not form bonds**

## 7.6 Metals, Nonmetals, and Metalloids

**Metals**: tend to form cations, luster, malleable, conductive (left side of the periodic table)

**Nonmetals**: tend to form anions, dull, brittle, nonconductive (right side of the periodic table)

**Metalloids**: intermediate properties (between metals and nonmetals)

**Summary**

# S2M-2 Part 2: Chemical Bonding (Chapter 8)

## Part 2: Chemical Bonding (Chapter 8)

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Midterm Chemistry S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Justin Lee 9-4. Editor: Justin Lee 9-4. Range: 7.4-8.7. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 8.1 Lewis Symbols and the Octet Rule

- A **chemical bond** is the electrostatic attraction that holds atoms together
  - **Ionic bond**: attraction between cations and anions
  - **Covalent bonds**: attraction between nucleus and shared electron pairs
  - **Metallic bond**: attraction between metal cations and delocalized electrons

**Octet Rule**

- All elements tend to reach **8 valence electrons** (stable noble gas configuration).

**Lewis Symbols**

- Consist of an element’s symbol + one dot per valence electron.

## 8.2 Ionic Bonding

**Definition**

- Ionic bond = electrostatic attraction between **cations (+)** and **anions (–)**.
- Formed by **complete electron transfer** from metal to nonmetal.

Cation Formation

- Metals (low electronegativity) lose valence electrons.
- Charge = Group 1A: +1; Group 2A: +2; Group 3A: +3.

Anion Formation (Negative Ions)

- Nonmetals (high electronegativity) gain electrons.
- Charge = group number – 8.

**Naming Ions** **(Monatomic)**

- **Cations**: same as element name (Na⁺ = sodium ion).
- **Anions**: element stem + -ide (Cl⁻ = chloride, O²⁻ = oxide).
- **Transition metals** **with multiple ions**: include Roman numeral for charge (Cu²⁺ = copper(II) Cu1+ = copper(II)).

**Writing Ionic Formulas (Crisscross Method)**

- Write cation symbol first, then anion symbol.
- Swap charge values to become subscripts.
- Reduce to the **lowest wholenumber ratio**.
  - **Ionic compounds don’t have discrete units**

**Properties of Ionic Compounds**

- High melting/boiling points (due to strong electrostatic attraction)
- Hard and brittle
- Conduct electricity **only when molten or dissolved in water**
- Exist as crystal lattices; basic unit = **formula unit**

**Lattice Energy**

- Definition: energy required to separate 1 mole of ionic solid into gaseous ions.
  - Higher ion charge or smaller ionic radius→ higher lattice energy
  - Smaller ion size or larger ionic radius→ higher lattice energy
  - **Covalent Bonding**

**Definition**: electrostatic attraction between **shared electrons** and atomic nuclei.

- Forms between nonmetal atoms

**Single, Double, Triple Covalent Bonds**

- **Single bond**: 1 shared pair (1 σ bond)
- **Double bond**: 2 shared pairs (1 σ + 1 π bond)
- **Triple bond**: 3 shared pairs (1 σ + 2 π bonds)

**Bond Length and Bond Energy**

- Shorter bond = stronger bond
- Bond length: **triple < double < single**
- Bond energy: **triple > double > single**

**Bond Dissociation Energy**

- Definition: energy needed to break 1 mole of a covalent bond.

**Molecular vs. Ionic Compounds**

| **Molecular Compounds** | **Ionic Compounds** |
|---|---|
| Nonmetal+Nonmetal | Metal+Metal |
| Molecule (discrete units) | Formula Unit (no discrete units) |
| Lower Melting Point | Higher Melting Point |
| Formula cannot be written in the simplest whole number ratio (HO and H2O2 are different) | Formula can only be written in the simplest whole number ratio |
| Weaker bonds | Stronger bonds |

## 8.4 Bond Polarity and Electronegativity

**Bond Polarity**

**Definition**: a measure of how unequally two atoms share the electrons in a covalent bond

- comes from a difference in electronegativity between the two bonded atoms.
- Nonpolar covalent: electrons shared equally (ΔEN ≤ 0.4)
- Polar covalent: electrons shared unequally (0.4 < ΔEN < 2.0)
- Ionic: electron transfer (ΔEN ≥ 2.0)

## 8.5 Drawing Lewis Structures

**StepbyStep Method**

- Calculate **total valence electrons** of all atoms.
- Put the central atom in the middle (usually the least electronegative atom except for hydrogen) and terminal atoms around it
- Connect atoms with single bonds.
- Complete octets for all terminal atoms.
- Assign remaining electrons to the central atom.
- Add double/triple bonds if the central atom does not have an octet.

**when more than 1 structure is valid, consider the structure with minimum formal charge**

**when more than 1 structure is valid AND those structures have the same formal charge, consider the structure that puts the negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom OR the structure that is symmetrical (more stable)**

  - **Resonance Structures**

**Definition**: Two or more valid Lewis structures for the same molecule/ion.

- When there are multiple Lewis structures possible, draw all of them and put an arrow between to indicate the resonance strcture
- HOWEVER, in reality, molecules with resonance structure do not match the extreme case shown above
- instead, the electron pair is delocalized and is in a freely moving state
- so, all bonds in the structure are equal (no clear single/double bonds) and have bond lengths that is short than single bonds but longer than double bonds

## 8.7 Exceptions to the Octet Rule

Three common exceptions:

- **Incomplete octets**
  - Fewer than 8 electrons (ex: Be, B).
- **Expanded octets**
  - More than 8 electrons (elements in period 3 and below has access to dorbitals).
- **Oddelectron molecules (free radicals)**
  - Unpaired electron; cannot satisfy octet (ex: NO, NO₂).

# S2F-1 PART 1: CHAPTER 7 FOUNDATIONS

## PART 1: CHAPTER 7 FOUNDATIONS

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Chemistry S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Calvin 9-9. Editor: Hanna Liu 9-6. Range: till 9.6, including periodic trends, ionic/metallic/covalent bond, naming compounds/writing formula unit and chemical formula, Lewis symbol and structure, formal charge, resonance structure, expanded octet, odd number ones, electron domain geometry and molecular geometry, hybridization, sigma and pi bond, bond polarity and molecular polarity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

## 1.1 Effective Nuclear Charge (Zₑff)

In a many-electron atom, each electron is simultaneously attracted to the nucleus (positive) and repelled by other electrons (negative). The net attractive force acting on an electron is defined as effective nuclear charge (Zₑff).

> **Key Definition: Effective Nuclear Charge**
> **Zₑff= Z − S**
> Where Z = actual nuclear charge (atomic number), S = shielding constant (total number of core electrons that shield valence electrons)

The shielding effect is the repelling effect that inner (core) electrons have on outer (valence) electrons, reducing the pull of the nucleus on valence electrons.

**Key rules for** **Zₑff** **trends:**

- Across a period (left → right): INCREASES(more protons, electrons fill the same shell; shielding stays nearly unchanged)
- Down a group (top → bottom): SLIGHTLY INCREASES (diffuse core electron clouds provide weak shielding)
- Same energy level: Zₑff order: s > p > d > f (s electrons lie closest to the nucleus)

### 1.2 Atomic and Ionic Radius

The bonding atomic radius is defined as one-half of the distance between two covalently bonded nuclei of the same element. It is a measure of how large an atom is.

**Atomic radius trends:**

- Across a period (left to right): radius DECREASES — more protons increase Zₑff, pulling electrons in closer despite being in the same shell.
- Down a group: radius INCREASES — each new period adds a new electron shell, greatly increasing distance from nucleus, and inter-electron repulsion grows.

Exception: Atomic radii of transition metals decrease much more slowly, as d electrons provide weak shielding.

**Ionic radius rules:**

- Cations < parent atoms: Losing electrons REDUCES repulsion, <mark>so</mark> electrons are pulled tighter by higher Zₑff.
- Anions > parent atoms: Gaining electrons INCREASES repulsion and expands the electron cloud.
- Down a group: Ionic radius INCREASES larger principal quantum number (n).
- Isoelectronic ions (same total electrons): radius DECREASES as nuclear charge rises.Example: O2−>F−>Na+>Mg2+ (all have 10 electrons)

### 1.3 Ionization Energy (IE)

Ionization energy (IE) is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion in its ground state. This process is always endothermic (positive energy value)

because you must overcome the attraction between the electron and the nucleus.

**Trends in 1st Ionization Energy:**

- Across a period (left to right): IE generally INCREASES (greater Zₑff means electrons are held more tightly.)
- Down a group: IE DECREASES (valence electrons are further from nucleus and more shielded, so easier to remove.)

**Two key exceptions to the left-to-right increase:**

- Group IIA → IIIA (e.g., Mg → Al): Slight DROP because Al loses an electron from a 3p orbital (higher energy, easier to remove) while Mg loses from 3s.
- Group VA → VIA (e.g., N → O): Slight DROP because O must remove an electron from a doubly-occupied orbital. Paired electrons repel each other, making one easier to remove.

### 1.4 Electronegativity (EN)

### Electronegativity refers to an atom’s ability to attract bonding electrons within a compound. It DIFFERS from ionization energy, which describes electron removal from isolated atoms.

Linus Pauling developed the most widely used electronegativity scale (dimensionless, ~0.7 to 4.0).

- **Most electronegative element: Fluorine (F) = 3.98**
- **Least electronegative element: Francium (Fr) ≈ 0.7**

**EN Trends**

Across a period (left → right): INCREASES (more protons pull bonding electrons more strongly)

Down a group (top → bottom): DECREASES (valence electrons further from nucleus, less attraction for bonding electrons).

# S2F-2 PART 2: CHAPTER 8 FOUNDATIONS

## PART 2: CHAPTER 8 FOUNDATIONS

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Chemistry S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Calvin 9-9. Editor: Hanna Liu 9-6. Range: till 9.6, including periodic trends, ionic/metallic/covalent bond, naming compounds/writing formula unit and chemical formula, Lewis symbol and structure, formal charge, resonance structure, expanded octet, odd number ones, electron domain geometry and molecular geometry, hybridization, sigma and pi bond, bond polarity and molecular polarity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

### 2.1 Lewis Symbols and the Octet Rule

A Lewis symbol for an element consists of the chemical symbol plus one dot for each valence electron.

The octet rule states that atoms tend to form bonds to achieve 8 valence electrons.

### 2.2 Bond Types — Ionic, Covalent, Metallic

The type of bond formed between two atoms depends primarily on the difference in electronegativity (ΔEN) between them.

| **Electronegativity Difference** | **Bond Type** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| ΔEN ≤ 0.4 | Nonpolar Covalent | Cl₂, N₂, H₂, C-H bonds |
| 0.4 < ΔEN < 2.0 | Polar Covalent | HCl (ΔEN=0.9), H₂O, NH₃ |
| ΔEN ≥ 2.0 | Ionic | NaCl (ΔEN=2.1), MgO |
| Metal + Metal | Metallic | Na metal, Cu wire, steel |

### 2.3 Drawing Lewis Structures

Lewis structures show all valence electrons as dots or lines (bonding pairs as lines, lone pairs as dots). Mastering this is CRITICAL for Chapter 9, since VSEPR and hybridization are both based on Lewis structures.

> **5-Step Guide to Drawing Lewis Structures**
> Step 1: Count total valence electrons. (Add 1 e⁻ per negative charge; subtract 1 per positive charge)
> Step 2: Choose central atom (forms most bonds). (H) is always a terminal atom.
> Step 3: Connect surrounding atoms to the central atom with single bonds. Each bond uses 2 electrons.
> Step 4: Complete octets of surrounding atoms (except H — give it 2).
> Step 5: Place remaining electrons on the central atom. If central atom lacks an octet, form double or triple bonds by relocating lone pairs from surrounding atoms.

> **Example: Lewis Structure of CO₂**
> Step 1: Valence electrons = C(4) + O(6) + O(6) = 16 total
> Step 2: C is central (less electronegative than O)
> Step 3: O-C-O with single bonds uses 4 electrons (12 left)
> Step 4: Give each O 3 lone pairs (uses 12 electrons). C has only 2 bonds = 4 electrons. Needs 4 more!
> **Step 5: Move 1 lone pair from each O → C to form double bonds: O=C=O**
> Final: :O=C=O: Each O has 2 lone pairs, C has no lone pairs. All octets satisfied. Total electrons used: 16 ✓

### 2.4 Formal Charge

Formal charge (FC) helps choose the best Lewis structure when multiple valid structures exist. It assumes electrons in bonds are shared EQUALLY between the bonded atoms.

> **Formal Charge Formula**
> **Formal Charge = (Valence electrons of neutral atom) − (Non-bonding electrons) − ½(Bonding electrons)**
> Or: FC = V − N − B/2
> The best Lewis structure: (1) minimizes formal charges on all atoms, (2) puts negative FC on more electronegative atoms, (3) has total FC equal to the ion charge (or zero for neutral molecules).

> **Example 2.4: Formal Charge in CO₂**
> **In O=C=O (two double bonds):**
> C: V=4, N=0 lone pairs, B=8 bonding electrons → FC = 4 - 0 - 4 = 0
> Each O: V=6, N=4 (2 lone pairs), B=4 bonding electrons → FC = 6 - 4 - 2 = 0
> **All formal charges = 0 → This is the BEST structure!**
> Compare with single bond O–C≡O: left O has FC=-1, right O has FC=+1 → not ideal because negative FC is on less electronegative C side.

### 2.5 Resonance Structures

When more than one valid Lewis structure can be written for a molecule or ion, differing only in the placement of electrons (not atoms), these are called resonance structures. The actual molecule is a resonance hybrid — a blend of all resonance structures.

**Key features of resonance:**

- All bonds in a resonance-stabilized structure are equivalent.

### 2.6 Exceptions to the Octet Rule

Three categories of exceptions exist — understanding them is critical because Chapter 9 features molecules like SF₆and PCl₅with expanded octets.

| **Exception Type** | **Explanation** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Odd electron (radical) | Molecules with an odd total number of valence electrons cannot follow the octet rule for all atoms. | NO (11 electrons), NO₂ (17 electrons), ClO₂ |
| Fewer than 8 electrons | Some elements in Period 2 with few electrons form stable molecules before filling an octet. | BF₃ (B has 6 electrons), BeCl₂ (Be has 4 electrons) |
| Expanded octet (> 8 e⁻) | Elements from Period 3 onwards can use empty d-orbitals, allowing the central atom to hold more than 8 valence electrons (expanded octet). | PCl₅ (10 e⁻ on P), SF₆ (12 e⁻ on S), XeF₄ (12 e⁻ on Xe) |

### 2.7 Bond Properties: Bond Order, Length, and Energy

These bond properties are the link between Chapter 8 and Chapter 9's discussion of hybrid orbitals and multiple bonds.

| **Property** | **Definition** | **Relationship** |
|---|---|---|
| Bond Order | Number of shared electron pairs between two atoms | Single=1, Double=2, Triple=3 |
| Bond Length | Distance between two bonded nuclei at minimum energy | Single > Double > Triple (LONGER) |
| Bond Energy | Energy required to break one mole of bonds in gas phase | Single < Double < Triple (STRONGER) |
| Sigma (σ) bond | Formed by head-on orbital overlap with cylindrical electron density symmetry. | All single bonds; 1 in each double/triple bond |
| Pi (π) bond | Formed by sideways overlap of parallel p-orbitals; electron density lies above and below the bond axis. | 1 in double bond; 2 in triple bond |

### 2.8 Chemical Bonding (Ionic, Covalent, Metallic)

### 2.8.1 Ionic Bonding

Electrostatic attraction between cations (+) and anions (−); formed by electron transfer.

It forms between metals + nonmetals (large electronegativity difference ≥ 2.0).

**Ion Formation:**

- Cation: Metals lose valence electrons. Transition metals form multiple cations (use Roman numerals).
- Anion: Nonmetals gain electrons; charge = group number − 8. Suffix changes to -ide.

**Key Properties:**

High melting/boiling points, hard & brittle.

Solid: non-conductive; molten/aqueous: conductive.

Exist as formula units (simplest ion ratio).

Lattice Energy:

Energy to separate 1 mol solid ionic compound into gaseous ions.

Higher ion charge / smaller ion size → larger lattice energy → stronger ionic bond.

## 2.8.2 Covalent Bonding

Electrostatic attraction between shared valence electrons and atomic nuclei; formed by electron sharing.

Formed by electron sharing between nonmetals (ΔEN < 2.0).

- More shared pairs → shorter bond length → higher bond energy
- Larger atoms → longer, weaker bonds

**Two Covalent Structures**

1. Molecular covalent: Discrete molecules, weak intermolecular forces, low melting/boiling points.

2. Giant (network) covalent: Atoms bonded by continuous covalent bonds, extremely high melting points.

**Octet Rule Exceptions**

1. Odd valence electrons

2. Less than 8 electrons

3. Expanded octet (3rd period & below, use d-orbitals; e.g. PCl5, SF6).

**2.8.3. Metallic Bonding**

Attraction between metal cations and delocalized "sea of valence electrons".

Exists in pure metals and metal alloys.

**Key Properties**

Good thermal & electrical conductivity (free moving electrons).

Malleable & ductile (cations slide easily, and no repulsion).

Most are solid at room temperature (exception: Hg = liquid), metallic luster.

**Bond Strength**

↑ delocalized electrons + ↓ ionic radius = ↑ metallic bonds = ↑ melting points.

## 2.9 Naming Chemical Compounds and Formulas

**Binary Ionic (Metal + Single Nonmetal Ion):**

Rules：

1. Name cation first (same as element name).

2. Name anion with suffix -ide.

3. Transition metals (multiple charges): add Roman numeral for cation charge.

Formula Writing: Balance total positive and negative charges (crisscross method).

**Ionic Compounds with Polyatomic Ions:**

Polyatomic ions act as one unit, and use parentheses if more than one is needed.

**Suffix rules for oxyanions:**

- -ate: more oxygen; -ite: less oxygen
- per- + -ate: most oxygen; hypo- + -ite: fewest oxygen

**Binary Molecular Compounds (Two Nonmetals):**

Prefixes:mono(1), di(2), tri(3), tetra(4), penta(5), hexa(6)…

Rules:

1. Use prefixes for each element and omit mono- for the first element.

2. Second element ends with -ide.

# S2F-3 PART 3: CHAPTER 9

## PART 3: CHAPTER 9

> From the Grade 9 Resource Department's Semester 2 Final Chemistry S+ review guide (PA). Writers: Calvin 9-9. Editor: Hanna Liu 9-6. Range: till 9.6, including periodic trends, ionic/metallic/covalent bond, naming compounds/writing formula unit and chemical formula, Lewis symbol and structure, formal charge, resonance structure, expanded octet, odd number ones, electron domain geometry and molecular geometry, hybridization, sigma and pi bond, bond polarity and molecular polarity. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

### 3.1 Why Molecular Shape Matters

The shape of a molecule governs:

- Physical properties: boiling point, melting point, density, solubility (polar vs nonpolar solvents)
- Polarity: whether the molecule is polar or nonpolar depends on BOTH bond polarities AND geometry
- Biological function: enzyme active sites, drug-receptor binding, and protein folding all depend on molecular shape
- Reactivity: spatial arrangement of atoms determines how two molecules can approach each other to react

### 3.2 VSEPR Theory — Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion

VSEPR theory is the primary model for predicting molecular geometry. The core principle is simple but powerful:

> **VSEPR Core Principle**
> **Electron pairs (and electron domains) around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible, minimizing repulsion.**
> An ELECTRON DOMAIN = any region of electron density: a single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair each count as ONE domain, regardless of how many electrons are actually there.
> The DOMAIN GEOMETRY (electron geometry) = arrangement of ALL electron domains. The MOLECULAR SHAPE = arrangement of ATOMS only (ignoring lone pairs for naming).

**Repulsion strength (from strongest to weakest):**

- **Lone pair – Lone pair repulsion > Lone pair – Bonding pair > Bonding pair – Bonding pair**

This explains why lone pairs compress bond angles below the ideal geometry value.

> **Example: Why H₂O bond angle is 104.5° not 109.5°**
> H₂O has 4 electron domains (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) → tetrahedral electron domain geometry.
> Ideal tetrahedral bond angle = 109.5°
> But 2 lone pairs exert extra repulsion on the 2 O-H bonds, pushing them closer together.
> **Result: bond angle compresses to 104.5°. Compare NH₃ (1 lone pair): 107°. More lone pairs = smaller bond angles.**

#### 3.2.1 The 5 Basic Electron Domain Geometries

| **# Electron Domains** | **Domain Geometry** | **Ideal Bond Angles** |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Linear | 180° |
| 3 | Trigonal planar | 120° |
| 4 | Tetrahedral | 109.5° |
| 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | 90°, 120°, 180° |
| 6 | Octahedral | 90°, 180° |

#### 3.2.2 Complete VSEPR Shape Table

The molecular shape is derived from the electron domain geometry by noting how many of those domains are lone pairs vs bonding pairs.

| **Molecular Shape** | **Bonding Domains** | **Lone Pairs** | **Bond Angles** | **Examples** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linear | 2 | 0 | 180° | CO₂, CS₂, HCN | BeF₂ also (but lone pairs on Be is exception) |
| Trigonal planar | 3 | 0 | 120° | BF₃, BCl₃, CH₂O | B has only 6 e⁻ (exception to octet) |
| Bent | 2 | 1 | ~117.5° | SO₂, NO₂⁻, O₃ | 1 lone pair compresses bond angle slightly below 120° |
| Tetrahedral | 4 | 0 | 109.5° | CH₄, CCl₄, NH₄⁺ | Perfect symmetry, nonpolar if same surrounding atoms |
| Trigonal pyramidal | 3 | 1 | ~107° | NH₃, PCl₃, NF₃ | 1 lone pair compresses from 109.5° |
| Bent | 2 | 2 | ~104.5° | H₂O, H₂S, OF₂ | 2 lone pairs compress bond angle the most of tetrahedral-based shapes |
| Trigonal bipyramidal | 5 | 0 | 90°,120°,180° | PCl₅, PF₅ | Axial bonds (90°) and equatorial bonds (120°) are NOT equivalent |
| Seesaw | 4 | 1 | ~90°,~120° | SF₄, XeO₂F₂ | Lone pair in equatorial position (largest 'seat') |
| T-shaped | 3 | 2 | ~90°,180° | ClF₃, ICl₃ | 2 lone pairs in equatorial positions |
| Linear | 2 | 3 | 180° | XeF₂, I₃⁻ | 3 lone pairs in equatorial positions |
| Octahedral | 6 | 0 | 90°,180° | SF₆, MoF₆ | All bonds equivalent; highly symmetric |
| Square pyramidal | 5 | 1 | ~90° | IF₅, XeOF₄ | 1 lone pair on top or bottom |
| Square planar | 4 | 2 | 90° | XeF₄, ICl₄⁻ | 2 lone pairs opposite each other (180° apart) |

#### 3.2.3 VSEPR Procedure

> **How to Determine Molecular Shape — 4 Steps**
> Step 1: Draw the Lewis structure. Count total valence electrons carefully.
> Step 2: Count electron domains on the central atom. (lone pairs + bonds = total domains)
> Step 3: Identify the electron domain geometry from the 5 basic geometries.
> Step 4: Name the molecular shape based on atom positions only (ignore lone pairs). Estimate bond angles (compress by ~2.5° for each lone pair in tetrahedral family).

> **Example 3.2: Determine the shape of XeF₄**
> Step 1: Lewis structure: Xe is central. Total VE = 8 + 4(7) = 36. Place 4 Xe-F bonds (8 e⁻). Complete F octets (24 e⁻). Remaining: 36-8-24=4 e⁻ = 2 lone pairs on Xe.
> Step 2: Electron domains on Xe = 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 6 total domains
> Step 3: 6 electron domains → OCTAHEDRAL domain geometry
> **Step 4: 2 lone pairs arrange opposite each other (180°) to minimize lone pair-lone pair repulsion. The 4 F atoms form a square. Molecular shape = SQUARE PLANAR. Bond angles = 90°.**

#### 3.2.4 Shapes of Larger Molecules

For molecules with more than one central atom, determine the geometry around EACH central atom separately using VSEPR. The overall molecular shape is described by listing each atom's geometry.

> **Example 3.4: Larger molecule with two central atoms**
> **Consider CH₃CHO** **:**
> First carbon (CH₃): 4 single bonds, 0 lone pairs → TETRAHEDRAL (109.5°)
> Second carbon (CHO): 2 single bonds + 1 double bond (=O) = 3 domains → TRIGONAL PLANAR (120°)
> The overall molecule is NOT flat, because the CH₃ end is tetrahedral. Only the CHO end is planar.

### 3.3 Molecular Polarity

A polar molecule (also called a dipole) has a positive end and a negative end due to an uneven distribution of electron density. Whether a molecule is polar depends on TWO factors: bond polarity AND molecular geometry.

> **Key Rule for Molecular Polarity**
> **A molecule is POLAR if:**
> 1. It has polar bonds (ΔEN > 0), AND
> 2. The bond dipoles do NOT cancel each other out due to molecular geometry (asymmetric molecule).
> **A molecule is NONPOLAR if:**
> 1. All bonds are nonpolar (same elements), OR
> 2. It has polar bonds but they CANCEL perfectly due to symmetric geometry.

**Symmetric shapes where bond dipoles cancel (nonpolar IF all surrounding atoms are the same):**

- Linear (2 identical bonds): CO₂ , two C=O dipoles point opposite directions and cancel → NONPOLAR
- Trigonal planar (3 identical bonds): BF₃ , three B-F dipoles arranged 120° apart, vector sum = 0 → NONPOLAR
- Tetrahedral (4 identical bonds): CH₄ , four C-H dipoles cancel perfectly → NONPOLAR
- Trigonal bipyramidal (5 identical bonds): PCl₅ → NONPOLAR
- Octahedral (6 identical bonds): SF₆ → NONPOLAR
- Square planar (4 identical bonds): XeF₄ → NONPOLAR

**Asymmetric shapes where bond dipoles do NOT cancel (polar if bonds are polar):**

- Bent: H₂O , 2 lone pairs push the molecule into a V-shape; O-H dipoles add up, not cancel → POLAR
- Trigonal pyramidal: NH₃ , the lone pair on N means the N-H dipoles don't cancel → POLAR
- Seesaw, T-shaped, Square pyramidal: all have lone pairs creating asymmetry → typically POLAR

> **Example: Determine if CH₂Cl₂ is polar or nonpolar**
> Step 1: Lewis structure → C is central, bonded to 2 H and 2 Cl. 4 bonding domains, 0 lone pairs.
> Step 2: Molecular shape = TETRAHEDRAL (4 bonds, no lone pairs)
> Step 3: Bond polarity? C-H: ΔEN = 0.4 (barely polar). C-Cl: ΔEN = 0.5 (polar, Cl is more electronegative).
> Step 4: Even though the geometry is tetrahedral, the surrounding atoms are NOT all identical (2 H + 2 Cl). The C-Cl dipoles point toward Cl, and the C-H dipoles are weaker. The net dipole ≠ 0.
> **Conclusion: CH₂Cl₂ is POLAR. (Compare with CCl₄** **,** **4 identical C-Cl bonds in tetrahedral geometry → nonpolar)**

> **Example: XeF₄ (Square Planar)**
> XeF₄: octahedral domain geometry, 4 bonds, 2 lone pairs → SQUARE PLANAR molecular shape
> The 2 lone pairs are on OPPOSITE sides (top and bottom), canceling each other's effect.
> The 4 Xe-F bonds are in the same plane, 90° apart (opposite bonds cancel, adjacent bonds also cancel.)
> **Conclusion: XeF₄ is NONPOLAR despite having polar Xe-F bonds! The square planar geometry makes all bond dipoles cancel perfectly.**

### 3.4 Hybrid Orbitals (Section 9.5)

> **What is Hybridization?**
> Hybridization = the mixing of atomic orbitals on an atom to form a new set of 'hybrid' orbitals that are all equivalent in energy and shape.
> **Key rule: The NUMBER of hybrid orbitals formed = the number of atomic orbitals mixed.**
> **The hybridization of a central atom ALWAYS matches its electron domain geometry.**

#### 3.4.1 sp Hybridization (2 electron domains → LINEAR)

When 1 s orbital and 1 p orbital mix, they form 2 sp hybrid orbitals arranged at 180° (linear).

The 2 remaining unhybridized p orbitals are perpendicular to each other and to the bond axis.

> **sp Hybridization in BeF₂**
> Be ground state: [He] 2s² (no unpaired electrons — can't form bonds!)
> After sp hybridization: mix 2s + one 2p → 2 sp hybrids at 180° apart + 2 unhybridized p orbitals
> Each sp hybrid has 1 unpaired electron → forms σ bond with F
> **Result: BeF₂ is LINEAR with 180° bond angle ✓ (matches VSEPR prediction for 2 electron domains)**

#### 3.4.2 sp² Hybridization (3 electron domains → TRIGONAL PLANAR)

When 1 s orbital and 2 p orbitals mix, they form 3 sp² hybrid orbitals arranged at 120° (trigonal planar).

The 1 remaining unhybridized p orbital is perpendicular to the plane of the molecule and participates in π bonding.

> **sp² Hybridization in BF₃**
> B ground state: [He] 2s² 2p¹ (only 1 unpaired electron normally)
> After sp² hybridization: mix 2s + two 2p → 3 sp² hybrids at 120° apart + 1 unhybridized p orbital
> Each sp² hybrid forms a σ bond with F. B has only 6 electrons (exception to octet).
> **Result: BF₃ is TRIGONAL PLANAR with 120° bond angle ✓**

#### 3.4.3 sp³ Hybridization (4 electron domains → TETRAHEDRAL)

When 1 s orbital and 3 p orbitals mix, they form 4 sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged at 109.5° (tetrahedral).

> **sp³ in Molecules with Lone Pairs: NH₃ and H₂O**
> NH₃: N has 4 electron domains (3 bonds + 1 lone pair) → sp³ hybridized. 3 sp³ hybrids hold σ bonds with H; 1 sp³ hybrid holds the lone pair.
> H₂O: O has 4 electron domains (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs) → sp³ hybridized. 2 sp³ hybrids hold σ bonds with H; 2 sp³ hybrids hold lone pairs.
> **IMPORTANT: The hybridization is still sp³ for both! The lone pairs occupy sp³ orbitals just like the bonding pairs do. The MOLECULAR SHAPE is different (trigonal pyramidal for NH₃, bent for H₂O), but the HYBRIDIZATION is the same.**

#### 3.4.4 sp³d and sp³d² Hybridization (5 and 6 electron domains)

Elements in Period 3 and beyond can use d orbitals in hybridization, allowing 5 or 6 electron domains. This is why only Period 3+ elements form expanded octets.

| **Hybridization** | **Electron Domains** | **Domain Geometry & Angles** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| sp | 2 | Linear, 180° | BeF₂, CO₂, HCN, C₂H₂ |
| sp² | 3 | Trigonal planar, 120° | BF₃, C₂H₄, CH₂O, SO₃ (resonance hybrid) |
| sp³ | 4 | Tetrahedral, 109.5° | CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, CCl₄, PCl₃ |
| sp³d | 5 | Trigonal bipyramidal | PCl₅, SF₄, ClF₃, XeF₂ |
| sp³d² | 6 | Octahedral | SF₆, IF₅, XeF₄ |

#### 3.4.5 How to Determine Hybridization

> **Hybridization Shortcut**
> **Count the total number of electron domains on the central atom:**
> **2 domains → sp \| 3 domains → sp² \| 4 domains → sp³**
> **5 domains → sp³d \| 6 domains → sp³d²**
> Remember: electron DOMAINS include lone pairs! (domains = bonds + lone pairs)

> **Example 3.7: Determine hybridization of each atom in CH₂O (formaldehyde)**
> Lewis structure: H₂C=O → C has 3 electron domains (2 single bonds to H + 1 double bond to O)
> **C: 3 domains → sp² hybridized. The unhybridized p on C forms the π bond with O.**
> O: has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains → sp³ hybridized.
> In practice: treat each atom separately. C in C=O with no lone pairs has 3 domains → sp². The O bonded to C with double bond can be treated as sp² or sp³ depending on whether lone pairs are in hybrid or unhybridized orbitals (in this context, treat O as sp² since it participates in π bond).

> **Example 3.8: HCN**
> Lewis structure: H–C≡N (C has triple bond to N, single bond to H)
> **C: 2 electron domains (1 single bond to H + 1 triple bond to N) → sp hybridized**
> **N: 2 electron domains (1 triple bond to C + 1 lone pair) → sp hybridized**
> Molecular shape: LINEAR. Both C and N are sp hybridized. The triple bond consists of 1 σ bond (sp-sp overlap) + 2 π bonds (two perpendicular p-p sideways overlaps).

### 3.5 Multiple Bonds

Multiple bonds combine one sigma (σ) bond with one or more pi (π) bonds. Understanding this distinction is crucial for hybridization, resonance, and molecular geometry.

#### 3.5.1 Sigma (σ) Bonds

- Formed by direct (head-on) overlap of orbitals along the bond axis.
- Cylindrical symmetry of electron density around the internuclear axis.
- ALL single bonds are sigma bonds.
- Every double and triple bond contains exactly ONE sigma bond.
- Sigma bonds are FREE TO ROTATE, and this allows single bonds in a molecule to flex.
- Sigma bonds can be formed by: s-s, s-p, s-sp, sp-sp, sp-sp², sp²-sp², sp³-sp³, etc.

#### 3.5.2 Pi (π) Bonds

- Formed by sideways (lateral) overlap of two parallel p orbitals.
- Electron density is found ABOVE and BELOW the bond axis (in two lobes).
- WEAKER than sigma bonds (less overlap efficiency in sideways orientation).
- Pi bonds CANNOT rotate freely, so that rotation would destroy the sideways overlap.
- A double bond = 1 σ + 1 π. A triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π.
- **Pi bonds require unhybridized p orbitals to be available. It’s** **only possible if the central atom is sp or sp² hybridized (sp³ hybridization uses all p orbitals in hybridization, leaving none for π).**

> **Important:** **σ** **vs** **π** **Bond Summary**
> **Single bond: 1σ, 0π** **\| Double bond: 1σ, 1π** **\| Triple bond: 1σ, 2π**
> Count σ bonds: = number of single bonds + 1 for each double bond + 1 for each triple bond
> Count π bonds: = 0 for single bonds + 1 per double bond + 2 per triple bond
> In acetylene (H-C≡C-H): 3 σ bonds (H-C, C-C, C-H) + 2 π bonds (the 2 extra bonds in the triple bond)

#### 3.5.3 Resonance, Delocalization, and Pi Bonding

When resonance occurs, the π electrons are not confined to one location but spread (delocalize) over multiple atoms. This concept connects Chapter 8 resonance structures with the quantum mechanical reality of π bonding.

> **Delocalized π Bonding**
> Delocalization occurs when p orbitals on multiple adjacent atoms overlap, spreading the π electron density over the entire system rather than between just two atoms.
> Conditions for delocalization: ALL atoms in the sequence must have an unhybridized p orbital available (i.e., sp or sp² hybridized).
> **Evidence: all bonds in a resonance-stabilized structure have equal lengths and intermediate bond orders (greater than a single bond, less than a double bond).**

> **Example 3.10: Delocalized π bonding in NO₃⁻**
> N is sp² hybridized (3 electron domains: 1 double bond + 2 single bonds). Each O is also sp² hybridized.
> N has 1 unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the molecule. Each O ALSO has an unhybridized p orbital in the same plane (perpendicular orientation).
> All four p orbitals (N + 3 O) overlap side-by-side, creating a delocalized π system that spans ALL four atoms.
> **Result: 2 π electrons are spread equally over all 3 N-O bonds. Bond order = 1 + (2/6) ≈ 1.33 (between single and double). All 3 N-O bonds are identical — confirmed experimentally.**
